14	# Strength Peaks at 20-28, Declines ~1%/Year After 30 — And Lab vs. Competition Data Disagree at the Extremes
15	
16	**What it is** — Strength peaks between roughly ages 20-28 for both men and women, then
17	declines by approximately 1% per year. The text compares two measurement approaches:
18	laboratory isometric/isokinetic dynamometer data (Hettinger et al 1961; MacDougall et al
19	1982) versus real weightlifting competition performance across juvenile, junior, senior, and
20	Masters (40+) age-group records. The two datasets agree reasonably well through adolescence
21	but diverge at the extremes: lab measurements score prepubescent lifters *higher* than
22	competition data would suggest (attributed to weight-trained children being much stronger
23	than untrained peers of the same age, biasing the comparison), and lab measurements score
24	older lifters (55+) *higher* than their competition performance, attributed to Olympic
25	weightlifting's added demand for agility and strength-speed across multiple muscle groups,
26	versus dynamometer testing of one isolated muscle group (usually quadriceps). Linear
27	regression fits the 30-80 age decline for each dataset: for untrained lab subjects, %S =
28	120.17 - 0.68865A (R=0.988); for trained weightlifters, %S = 140.15 - 1.3853A (R=0.996),
29	where A is age in years — the steeper slope for trained lifters implies *more* absolute
30	decline per year for those who had reached a higher peak, even though both groups decline
31	by roughly the same fraction. A worked example combines this with the bodymass-adjustment
32	equations (3.3.5) to show a 45-year-old, 80 kg lifter with a 260 kg total (87.1%
33	age-and-bodymass-adjusted score) can have *greater* relative strength than a young 90 kg
34	lifter with a 350 kg total (86.3% bodymass-adjusted, no age adjustment needed) — illustrating
35	that raw totals alone can mask true relative-strength standing across ages. (PDF pp.
36	170-173, printed pp. 159-162, "3.3.7 The Relationship between Strength and Age,"
37	Table 3.6, Fig 3.25.)
38	
39	**Why it works** — No single mechanism is given for the underlying age-strength decline
40	itself (that is well-documented broadly in exercise-science, e.g. sarcopenia); the
41	explanation offered here is specifically for *why the two measurement methods disagree* at
42	the young and old extremes — differing skill/technical demands (isolated-joint dynamometer
43	testing vs. whole-body competitive lifting) mean the two methods are not measuring
44	identical constructs, especially where technical skill and multi-joint coordination (more
45	present in older, more experienced competitive lifters, and more absent in
46	still-developing young lifters) partially compensates for or masks the underlying raw
47	strength trend.
48	
49	**When to apply** — Use the disagreement-at-the-extremes finding to choose the right
50	measurement approach for the population in question: isolated dynamometer/force-plate
51	testing is likely to be a fairer read on very young or very old populations than
52	competition-style multi-joint lift performance, which conflates raw strength with
53	accumulated technical skill. **Inference:** for Baylor's mixed-age roster (true freshmen
54	through fifth-year seniors), this suggests raw 1RM comparisons across class years should be
55	read cautiously if technical proficiency in the tested lift itself differs systematically
56	by experience/class year, since that skill difference can move the number independent of
57	underlying strength.
58	
59	**When NOT to apply** — The specific regression equations are fit to weightlifting records
60	and a small number of lab studies (Hettinger 1961; MacDougall 1982) predating this text's
61	publication; the exact numeric coefficients (120.17, 0.68865, 140.15, 1.3853) should be
62	treated as illustrative of that era's data and that specific population, not as a precise,
63	individually-applicable age-adjustment formula for a current athlete population. This entry
64	does not claim the underlying decline pattern is independently confirmed beyond these
65	cited sources; no other source is named here to corroborate it.
66	
67	**Example** — Comparing a 22-year-old's and a 45-year-old assistant coach's back squat by
68	raw weight alone (or even bodymass-adjusted alone) undercounts the older lifter's relative
69	standing; applying both the bodymass adjustment (3.3.5) and the age adjustment (equation
70	3.9) together, as the book's own worked example does, can reverse which lifter actually has
71	the higher relative strength.
72	
73	**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the paired bodymass-adjustment
74	method this age adjustment is explicitly combined with).
75

# Strength Peaks at 20-28, Declines ~1%/Year After 30 — And Lab vs. Competition Data Disagree at the Extremes

**What it is** — Strength peaks between roughly ages 20-28 for both men and women, then
declines by approximately 1% per year. The text compares two measurement approaches:
laboratory isometric/isokinetic dynamometer data (Hettinger et al 1961; MacDougall et al
1982) versus real weightlifting competition performance across juvenile, junior, senior, and
Masters (40+) age-group records. The two datasets agree reasonably well through adolescence
but diverge at the extremes: lab measurements score prepubescent lifters *higher* than
competition data would suggest (attributed to weight-trained children being much stronger
than untrained peers of the same age, biasing the comparison), and lab measurements score
older lifters (55+) *higher* than their competition performance, attributed to Olympic
weightlifting's added demand for agility and strength-speed across multiple muscle groups,
versus dynamometer testing of one isolated muscle group (usually quadriceps). Linear
regression fits the 30-80 age decline for each dataset: for untrained lab subjects, %S =
120.17 - 0.68865A (R=0.988); for trained weightlifters, %S = 140.15 - 1.3853A (R=0.996),
where A is age in years — the steeper slope for trained lifters implies *more* absolute
decline per year for those who had reached a higher peak, even though both groups decline
by roughly the same fraction. A worked example combines this with the bodymass-adjustment
equations (3.3.5) to show a 45-year-old, 80 kg lifter with a 260 kg total (87.1%
age-and-bodymass-adjusted score) can have *greater* relative strength than a young 90 kg
lifter with a 350 kg total (86.3% bodymass-adjusted, no age adjustment needed) — illustrating
that raw totals alone can mask true relative-strength standing across ages. (PDF pp.
170-173, printed pp. 159-162, "3.3.7 The Relationship between Strength and Age,"
Table 3.6, Fig 3.25.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is given for the underlying age-strength decline
itself (that is well-documented broadly in exercise-science, e.g. sarcopenia); the
explanation offered here is specifically for *why the two measurement methods disagree* at
the young and old extremes — differing skill/technical demands (isolated-joint dynamometer
testing vs. whole-body competitive lifting) mean the two methods are not measuring
identical constructs, especially where technical skill and multi-joint coordination (more
present in older, more experienced competitive lifters, and more absent in
still-developing young lifters) partially compensates for or masks the underlying raw
strength trend.

**When to apply** — Use the disagreement-at-the-extremes finding to choose the right
measurement approach for the population in question: isolated dynamometer/force-plate
testing is likely to be a fairer read on very young or very old populations than
competition-style multi-joint lift performance, which conflates raw strength with
accumulated technical skill. **Inference:** for Baylor's mixed-age roster (true freshmen
through fifth-year seniors), this suggests raw 1RM comparisons across class years should be
read cautiously if technical proficiency in the tested lift itself differs systematically
by experience/class year, since that skill difference can move the number independent of
underlying strength.

# Strength Peaks at 20-28 and Declines About 1% a Year After 30: Lab and Competition Data Disagree at the Extremes

**What it is** — Strength peaks between roughly ages 20-28 for both men and women, then
declines by approximately 1% per year (PDF p. 170, printed p. 159). The text compares two
measurement approaches: laboratory isometric/isokinetic dynamometer data (Hettinger et al
1961; MacDougall et al 1982) versus real weightlifting competition performance across
juvenile, junior, senior, and Masters (over 40) age-group records (Table 3.6, PDF p. 171,
printed p. 160). The two datasets correspond reasonably well through adolescence but
diverge outside that range: below about age 14, lifting percentages run *higher* than lab
percentages (at age 10: lab 42%, lifting 59%), which the text attributes to weight-trained
children being much stronger than their untrained peers; over about 45 years, lifting
percentages fall *below* lab percentages (at age 65: lab 74%, lifting 49%), which the text
attributes to Olympic weightlifting's added demand for agility and strength-speed across
many muscle groups, versus dynamometer testing of one limited muscle group (usually the
quadriceps). Linear regression fits the 30-80 age decline separately for each dataset: for
untrained lab subjects, %S = 120.17 - 0.68865A (R=0.988); for trained weightlifters, %S =
140.15 - 1.3853A (R=0.996), where A is age in years and %S is the percentage of one's own
peak strength (eqs 3.8-3.9, printed 160). The trained-lifter curve declines about twice as
fast, in percentage-of-peak terms, as the untrained-lab curve, and neither coefficient
matches the "approximately 1% per annum" the same section states earlier (printed 159).
Record all three figures as given: the text does not reconcile them, and this entry does
not harmonize them either. (PDF pp. 170-171, printed pp. 159-160, "3.3.7 The Relationship
between Strength and Age," Table 3.6, Fig 3.25.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for the underlying age-strength decline itself.
**Inference:** this is broadly consistent with ordinary age-related neuromuscular decline,
though the text gives no citation for that and none is supplied here. For *why the two
measurement methods disagree* at the extremes, the text gives a stated reason at each end,
not a single unifying mechanism: below about 14, weight-trained children are simply much
stronger than untrained same-age peers, which biases the comparison at that end; over 45,
Olympic weightlifting's agility and strength-speed demands across many muscle groups pull
lifting scores below dynamometer scores at that end (printed 160). The authors do not
frame this as skill "masking" the older lifters' true underlying strength; they present
lab and lifting as two different measurements of different things, not one measurement
that is closer to the truth than the other.

**When to apply** — Use the disagreement-at-the-extremes finding to choose the right
measurement approach for the population in question: isolated dynamometer or force-plate
testing may better isolate raw strength for very young or very old populations, while
competition-style multi-joint lift performance folds in accumulated technical skill and,
at the older end, a different demand structure (agility, strength-speed) than raw strength
alone. **Inference:** for Baylor's mixed-age roster (true freshmen through fifth-year
seniors, and any over-45 staff testing), raw 1RM comparisons across class years should be
read cautiously if technical proficiency in the tested lift differs systematically by
experience or class year, since that skill difference can move the number independent of
underlying strength. This reasoning is rebuilt from the corrected direction of the
lab-versus-lifting disagreement above; an earlier draft of this entry had that direction
reversed.

14	# Training at a Joint's Longest-Muscle-Length Angle Transfers More Evenly; Training at a Shortened Angle Gains More but Transfers Less
15	
16	**What it is** — Citing Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1974) and Raitsin & Sarsania (1975),
17	Verkhoshansky states that where in the range of motion an athlete trains a single-joint
18	movement changes how that strength gain transfers to other joint angles. If maximum
19	muscular force is trained at the angle corresponding to the muscle's greatest length (the
20	smallest degree of flexion for active flexion work, or the least extension for extension
21	work), the resulting strength increase transfers relatively uniformly to other joint
22	angles. If maximum force is instead trained with the joint significantly flexed and the
23	muscle in a shortened state, the resulting strength increase at that specific angle is
24	larger, but transfers comparatively poorly to other joint angles, with transfer falling off
25	further the farther the target angle is from the trained one. (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp.
26	102-103.)
27	
28	**Why it works** — The author gives no cellular mechanism in this passage; he treats it as
29	an established empirical regularity from isometric training-at-a-single-angle studies. **Inference:**
30	a plausible mechanism (not stated in this passage) is that training at a lengthened position
31	recruits a joint-angle range closer to what most functional tasks pass through on the way to
32	lockout, so gains generalize across the arc, whereas training in a fully shortened position
33	trains a narrow, less commonly used part of the strength curve, producing a large but
34	narrowly-tuned adaptation (consistent with the general specificity principle in
35	[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]).
36	
37	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when deciding where in the range to bias a
38	strength exercise for an athlete who needs broad strength across a joint's full range (most
39	field-sport athletes) versus one who needs a large gain at one specific, narrow joint angle
40	that matches a single sport position (e.g. a very specific start-position strength need).
41	Favor training through, or anchored near, the lengthened position when general transfer
42	across a range of joint angles is the goal.
43	
44	**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from isometric single-joint training studies from the
45	1970s (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1974; Raitsin & Sarsania, 1975), not from dynamic, multi-joint,
46	or modern resistance-training methodology; **Inference:** do not assume this angle-specific
47	transfer pattern applies identically to dynamic full-range lifts (e.g. a full back squat),
48	where the muscle passes through many angles within a single repetition rather than training
49	isometrically at one fixed angle. The text also states the *shape* of the force-angle curve
50	itself does not change fundamentally with training, only the amount transferred across it,
51	so this claim is about magnitude of transfer, not about reshaping the underlying joint-angle
52	strength curve.
53	
54	**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete doing isometric mid-thigh-pull-style training near
55	a lengthened hip/knee position would be expected, per this claim, to show more even carryover
56	to strength expressed at other joint angles than an athlete who only trains isometric holds
57	in a deep, shortened flexed position, who would gain more at that specific angle but less
58	elsewhere.
59	
60	**Related** — [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]],
61	[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
62	[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]] (Chapter 1).

14	# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer
15	
16	**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
17	maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
18	to those points; Verkhoshansky reports that Siff's own research at the University of the
19	Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under non-isokinetic dynamic
20	conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the resulting dynamic force-angle
21	curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves obtained statically. The curve
22	profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and joint orientation: for example,
23	maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance) elbow flexion does not occur near
24	90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full flexion, and evoking the myotatic
25	stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension produces yet another profile. The
26	same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves versus curves measured under
27	unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in the chapter, Verkhoshansky
28	states directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are unable to measure functional
29	maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive strength," so it is "futile" to use
30	them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on sporting preparedness or progress. (PDF
31	pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15.)
32	
33	**Why it works** — Isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular
34	velocity, removing the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage/release, and
35	multi-joint coordination that dynamic sporting movements actually use; a device that
36	constrains those variables necessarily measures a different quality than the unconstrained,
37	explosive, multi-joint action it is often used to represent.
38	
39	**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
40	isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
41	not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
42	jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the department runs the isometric seated calf raise and
43	other isometric tests on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed
44	90-degree ankle/knee position (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
45	monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
46	**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
47	measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
48	alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
49	recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.
50	
51	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has
52	no value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
53	establish real, useful findings (e.g.
54	[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
55	testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance." The
56	caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests to infer dynamic,
57	functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all.
58	
59	**Example** — An athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
60	whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
61	sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak with a slow rate of force development, or measured
62	at the wrong joint angle for the sport skill, can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive

14	# Three Levels for Analyzing a Movement: Kinematic Pair, Kinematic Chain, Kinematic System
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky organizes movement analysis into three nested levels of
17	increasing complexity (PDF pp. 112-116, printed pp. 101-105): the **kinematic pair** (a
18	single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the
19	**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
20	knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
21	kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
22	together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
23	pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
24	a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for

# Three Levels for Analyzing a Movement: Kinematic Pair, Kinematic Chain, Kinematic System

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky organizes movement analysis into three nested levels of
increasing complexity (PDF pp. 112-116, printed pp. 101-105): the **kinematic pair** (a
single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the
**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base); at the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms
extend across a larger number of interacting muscle groups, chiefly the legs and torso
followed by the shoulder girdle.

**Why it works** — The author gives a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, he attributes the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

at the kinematic-pair level and, per this text, transfers narrowly; a compound lift like a

level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive analysis taxonomy, not a

14	# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky defines the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
17	all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
18	five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
19	force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
20	elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
21	of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
22	**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
23	reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
24	rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
25	physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
26	factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
27	irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
28	system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
29	variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
30	mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
31	pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
32	repetitive contributions. (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky
33	1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)
34	
35	**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
36	kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
37	repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
38	element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
39	dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
40	concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
41	linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
42	support that link.
43	
44	**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
45	why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
46	training means (see later chapters) should target which component: e.g. a movement that
47	depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) calls for plyometric or reactive
48	methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force (component 1) calls for
49	more conventional strength methods. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
50	reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
51	given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
52	lever.
53	
54	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
55	a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five
56	components separately in a real sports movement, so treat it as a way to structure thinking
57	about a movement's force sources, not as a set of directly testable variables. Do not confuse
58	"kinesiological pattern" with a simple biomechanical description of joint angles over time;
59	the term is explicitly meant to include the reflexive and adaptive character of the pattern,
60	which a purely kinematic (position/angle) analysis would miss.
61	
62	**Example** — In a vertical jump, the strength field includes the active quadriceps/glute
63	drive (component 1), ground reaction force (component 2), elastic energy stored during the
64	countermovement dip (component 3), the inertia of the body's mass being redirected (component
65	4), and body weight (component 5); an athlete with a weak amortization phase is likely
66	under-using component 3, which a purely strength-focused (component 1) training emphasis
67	would not fix.
68

71	[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1),

14	# Whether a Sport Rewards Fast Force (RFD) or Total Force/Momentum Should Decide Whether You Train Max Strength or Explosive Strength
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky illustrates with a thought experiment (Fig 2.14-2.15): two
17	athletes perform a maximal single repetition of the same exercise as fast as possible, then
18	hold the load until fatigue. Athlete B produces a greater maximum force and sustains force
19	longer overall (greater area under the curve, i.e. greater momentum and muscle endurance).
20	Athlete A, however, produces *more* force than B at any early instant before a crossover time
21	T2 (i.e. a faster Rate of Force Development). If the sport requires rapid RFD (jumping,
22	striking, throwing sports such as basketball, martial arts, track and field), athlete A has
23	the advantage, and training aimed at increasing athlete B's maximal strength or muscle bulk
24	would be "misdirected" for that goal; that athlete instead needs explosive-strength (RFD)
25	training. If the sport instead requires high maximal force or momentum regardless of timing
26	(wrestling, powerlifting, rugby scrumming, judo), athlete B has the advantage, and athlete A
27	will not improve without training to increase maximal strength. (PDF pp. 120-121, printed pp.
28	109-110.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — Maximal force and Rate of Force Development are separable qualities
31	because most sporting actions occur inside a limited time window; an athlete can be strong
32	in the sense of high peak force yet slow to reach it, or fast to reach a moderate force level
33	without a high ceiling. Matching training to which of these two qualities the sport actually
34	uses avoids spending training time raising a quality (say, 1RM strength) that the sport's time
35	constraints never let the athlete express (see
36	[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]], Chapter 1, for the
37	underlying, broadly-replicated basis of this distinction).
38	
39	**When to apply** — Use this as a first screening question when assigning a training
40	emphasis: does this athlete's sport-critical action reward reaching a given force level fast
41	(most acyclic, ballistic, and reactive football actions: block shed, first-step acceleration,
42	change of direction) or reward sustained/maximal force output regardless of speed
43	(sustained drive-block engagement, some wrestling-style contact)? **Eric's baseline:** force
44	plate reporting already separates driver metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force) from
45	strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations) under the ODSF framework rather than reporting a
46	single peak-force number (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"
47	citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this principle supports reading those driver and
48	strategy metrics specifically for RFD-type signal (how fast, not just how much) when deciding
49	whether an athlete's programming should lean toward explosive-strength or maximal-strength
50	work.
51	
52	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a two-athlete illustration, not a controlled
53	study, and most football positions and actions are not purely RFD-limited or purely
54	force/momentum-limited; a single football play often requires both (e.g. an offensive lineman
55	needs fast initial force application off the snap AND sustained drive force through the
56	block). Do not use this principle to justify training only one quality at the expense of the
57	other for a position that plainly needs both; use it to set relative emphasis, not to
58	eliminate either quality from a program.
59	
60	**Example** — A cornerback whose sport-critical actions (backpedal-to-break, closing speed)
61	are almost entirely time-limited would, per this principle, get more value from
62	explosive-strength/RFD-focused training than from chasing a higher back squat 1RM once a
63	baseline strength level is established; a nose tackle whose job includes anchoring against
64	sustained double-team drive would get more value from continuing to raise maximal strength.
65

68	[[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]] (Chapter 1).

13	
14	# Map an Athlete's Strength "Topography" (Dynamometric/Functional Profile) to Find Underdeveloped Muscle Groups
15	
16	**What it is** — Citing Uflyand (1965) and his own data, Verkhoshansky describes building a
17	**dynamometric profile**: a visual map of the maximal strength of a representative set of
18	muscle groups for a given athlete (Fig 2.16 shows this for high jump versus distance running,
19	across trunk extension/flexion, thigh extension, ankle plantar/dorsiflexion). A **general
20	dynamometric profile**, built across many athletes of one specialization, characterizes the
21	strength topography typical of that sport and is preserved as sports mastery increases within
22	that group (Semyenov et al, 1971), though the exact rate of development for individual muscle
23	groups still varies. Because athletes with near-identical dynamometric profiles can still
24	produce very different competitive results (e.g. two sprinters with equal relative strength
25	running 12.1s versus 12.4s), Verkhoshansky extends this to a **functional profile**
26	(sometimes called a "polyfunctional profile"), which adds the sport-relevant *speed*
27	qualities of each muscle group (how fast each group develops working force, not just its
28	peak) on top of the raw strength topography. (PDF pp. 121-123, printed pp. 110-112, Figs
29	2.16-2.18.)
30	
31	**Why it works** — A profile organized by muscle group and quality (strength peak, and
32	separately, speed of force development) exposes which specific groups are underdeveloped
33	relative to a sport's typical topography, which a single whole-body strength number cannot
34	show; adding the speed-of-development dimension captures why two athletes with equal peak
35	strength can still differ in performance, since the sport may reward how fast that strength
36	is expressed more than its ceiling (see
37	[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]]).
38	
39	**When to apply** — Use a per-muscle-group strength and RFD profile, benchmarked against
40	data from the athlete's own sport/position when available, to identify specific weak links
41	to target in programming, rather than programming purely off a general strength test.
42	**Eric's baseline:** the current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch,
43	ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis names as a real

# Map an Athlete's Strength "Topography" (Dynamometric/Functional Profile) to Find Underdeveloped Muscle Groups

**What it is** — Citing Uflyand (1965) and his own data, Verkhoshansky describes building a
**dynamometric profile**: a visual map of the maximal strength of a representative set of
muscle groups for a given athlete (Fig 2.16 shows this for high jump versus distance running,
across trunk extension/flexion, thigh extension, ankle plantar/dorsiflexion). A **general
dynamometric profile**, built across many athletes of one specialization, characterizes the
strength topography typical of that sport and is preserved as sports mastery increases within
that group (Semyenov et al, 1971), though the exact rate of development for individual muscle
groups still varies. Because athletes with near-identical dynamometric profiles can still
produce very different competitive results (e.g. two sprinters with equal relative strength
running 12.1s versus 12.4s), Verkhoshansky extends this to a **functional profile**
(sometimes called a "polyfunctional profile"), which adds the sport-relevant *speed*
qualities of each muscle group (how fast each group develops working force, not just its
peak) on top of the raw strength topography. (PDF pp. 121-123, printed pp. 110-112, Figs
2.16-2.18.)

**Why it works** — A profile organized by muscle group and quality (strength peak, and
separately, speed of force development) exposes which specific groups are underdeveloped
relative to a sport's typical topography, which a single whole-body strength number cannot
show; adding the speed-of-development dimension captures why two athletes with equal peak
strength can still differ in performance, since the sport may reward how fast that strength
is expressed more than its ceiling (see
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]]).

**When to apply** — Use a per-muscle-group strength and RFD profile, benchmarked against
data from the athlete's own sport/position when available, to identify specific weak links
to target in programming, rather than programming purely off a general strength test.
**Eric's baseline:** the current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch,
ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis names as a real
usability problem, with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data dictionaries listed as
priority unfinished work (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2`). **Inference:** this framework is
a direct conceptual match for that stated gap: a sport-specific dynamometric/functional
profile (per position group, not just per vendor) is essentially what the Development Plan's
proposed sport-specific data dictionary would need to support if it is to identify individual
athletes' weak links rather than just report raw device output; this specific mapping is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** building a useful general profile for a sport requires
a reasonably sized sample of athletes at that sport and level to establish what topography is
typical, which most single-team programs (including a college football roster split across
many position groups) will struggle to establish rigorously; a "general profile" built from a
handful of athletes risks reflecting individual variation rather than a real sport-typical
pattern. This is also a resource-intensive, multi-muscle-group testing approach; **Eric's
baseline** elsewhere states inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data and that
data collection has to be judged on cost versus insight (`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy
and decision principles," citing `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`,
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); a full multi-joint dynamometric battery would need to
clear that same cost-versus-insight bar before being added to an already-running testing
menu.

**Example** — Two running backs with equal 1RM back squats and equal CMJ height could still
differ in acceleration if one shows a slower rate of force development specifically at hip
extension; a functional profile built from isometric or force-plate testing at each major
joint action would surface that difference, where a single squat-max or jump-height number
would not.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]] (Chapter 1).

# The Force-Time Curve Changes a Specific Way With Long-Term Training, and the Pattern Differs by Movement Type

**What it is** — As sports proficiency grows, an athlete's force-time curve F(t) and
force-displacement curve F(s) change in a consistent overall pattern: the time to reach
maximal force decreases, maximal force increases, the point of maximal effort moves closer
to the start of muscle tension, and the total duration of the effort decreases. Verkhoshansky
cites his own longitudinal data (a leg-extension task, before and after 6 months of
training) and several other Soviet studies of athletes at different qualification levels as
support (PDF pp. 109-110, printed pp. 98-99, Figs 2.1-2.3). He then describes four distinct
sub-patterns by movement type, all sharing that same general trend but differing in where
force concentrates over the range of motion:
- **Large-resistance movements** (gymnastics, wrestling, weightlifting): perfecting is
  realised mainly by increasing maximum force with some decrease in time to produce it.
- **Ballistic/small-resistance movements** (fencing, some throwing): force concentrates near
  the *beginning* of the movement, shifting earlier and taking less time as mastery grows.
- **Stretch-shortening movements** (jumping, figure skating, acrobatics): perfecting comes
  from improving the muscles' ability to generate force during the eccentric-to-concentric
  transition, which shortens the working amplitude (a smaller joint-flexion angle) as
  mastery grows.
- **Cyclic movements** (running, swimming, rowing): perfecting comes from producing maximum
  force faster out of a deep, rapid relaxation phase, with a relatively longer relaxation
  phase and a shorter absolute cycle duration.
(PDF pp. 110-111, printed pp. 99-100, Figs 2.4-2.7.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no single unified mechanism for why the curve
reshapes this way across all four movement types; he attributes it to the general
perfecting of neuromuscular coordination and the kinesiological pattern (see
[[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]]) rather than a single
physiological cause. **Inference:** the shared trend (faster force onset, higher peak,
shorter total duration) is consistent with well-replicated modern findings that RFD and
neural drive improve with resistance training independent of large hypertrophy changes,
which would explain the timing shift; the movement-specific location of where force
concentrates is better explained by task constraints (available time, external resistance,
and whether the movement uses a stretch-shortening cycle) shaping which part of the range
the nervous system learns to emphasize.

**When to apply** — Use this as a framework for reading a force-time curve (e.g. a CMJ or
squat-jump trace from ForceDecks) against the athlete's event demands: a lineman's drive
block or a powerlifting-style movement should be read against the "large-resistance"
pattern (rising peak force, tightening time-to-peak), while a jump or plant-and-cut action
should be read against the "stretch-shortening" pattern (a shortening, more efficient
amortization). **Eric's baseline:** the department already runs the full ForceDecks CMJ
family and reports driver metrics like braking/propulsive force and phase durations under
the ODSF framework (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this framework
gives a training-adaptation lens for interpreting a trend in those phase-duration and
force metrics over a training block (e.g. a shortening amortization phase across a training
cycle) as a sign of the expected stretch-shortening-cycle adaptation, not just a data point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive pattern of *change over
training time*, not a same-day diagnostic; a single force-time trace cannot show whether an
athlete's curve is "improving" without a comparable baseline trace from earlier in that
athlete's training history. The four movement-type categories are the book's own taxonomy,
built from a handful of Soviet studies (Verkhoshansky 1961, 1963; Papysheva 1966; Gomberazde
1970; Semyenov 1970; Tatyan 1974) rather than a broad modern meta-analysis, so treat the
specific shapes (not just the general trend) as `supported`, not `proven`. Do not assume
every sport fits cleanly into one category; many football positions blend large-resistance
demands (line play) with stretch-shortening and cyclic demands (change of direction,
sprinting) within the same athlete.

**Example** — A running back's CMJ force-time trace, tracked across an off-season block,
would be expected (per this framework) to show a shortening, more front-loaded braking
phase and a higher, earlier propulsive peak as reactive strength improves, distinct from an
offensive lineman whose relevant curve (a drive-block or isometric mid-thigh pull trace)
would be expected to show a rising peak force with a flatter, less time-compressed profile.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1, the SEC mechanism behind
the stretch-shortening pattern here).

# Training at a Joint's Longest-Muscle-Length Angle Transfers More Evenly; Training at a Shortened Angle Gains More but Transfers Less

**What it is** — Citing Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1974) and Raitsin & Sarsania (1975),
Verkhoshansky states that where in the range of motion an athlete trains a single-joint
movement changes how that strength gain transfers to other joint angles. If maximum
muscular force is trained at the angle corresponding to the muscle's greatest length (the
smallest degree of flexion for active flexion work, or the least extension for extension
work), the resulting strength increase transfers relatively uniformly to other joint
angles. If maximum force is instead trained with the joint significantly flexed and the
muscle in a shortened state, the resulting strength increase at that specific angle is
larger, but transfers comparatively poorly to other joint angles, with transfer falling off
further the farther the target angle is from the trained one. (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp.
102-103.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no cellular mechanism in this passage; he treats it as
an established empirical regularity from isometric training-at-a-single-angle studies. **Inference:**
a plausible mechanism (not stated in this passage) is that training at a lengthened position
recruits a joint-angle range closer to what most functional tasks pass through on the way to
lockout, so gains generalize across the arc, whereas training in a fully shortened position
trains a narrow, less commonly used part of the strength curve, producing a large but
narrowly-tuned adaptation (consistent with the general specificity principle in
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when deciding where in the range to bias a
strength exercise for an athlete who needs broad strength across a joint's full range (most
field-sport athletes) versus one who needs a large gain at one specific, narrow joint angle
that matches a single sport position (e.g. a very specific start-position strength need).
Favor training through, or anchored near, the lengthened position when general transfer
across a range of joint angles is the goal.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from isometric single-joint training studies from the
1970s (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1974; Raitsin & Sarsania, 1975), not from dynamic, multi-joint,
or modern resistance-training methodology; **Inference:** do not assume this angle-specific
transfer pattern applies identically to dynamic full-range lifts (e.g. a full back squat),
where the muscle passes through many angles within a single repetition rather than training
isometrically at one fixed angle. The text also states the *shape* of the force-angle curve
itself does not change fundamentally with training, only the amount transferred across it,
so this claim is about magnitude of transfer, not about reshaping the underlying joint-angle
strength curve.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete doing isometric mid-thigh-pull-style training near
a lengthened hip/knee position would be expected, per this claim, to show more even carryover
to strength expressed at other joint angles than an athlete who only trains isometric holds
in a deep, shortened flexed position, who would gain more at that specific angle but less
elsewhere.

**Related** — [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]] (Chapter 1).

# Three Levels for Analyzing a Movement: Kinematic Pair, Kinematic Chain, Kinematic System

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky organizes movement analysis into three nested levels of
increasing complexity (PDF pp. 112-116, printed pp. 101-105): the **kinematic pair** (a
single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the
**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base); at the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms
extend across a larger number of interacting muscle groups, chiefly the legs and torso
followed by the shoulder girdle.

**Why it works** — The author gives a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, he attributes the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to decide what level of analysis (and therefore what
level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level and, per this text, transfers narrowly; a compound lift like a
clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even
single-chain exercise. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection is already organized on a
general-to-specific spectrum (general preparation, specific preparation, specific
development, competitive exercises, per Bondarchuk) and weighted toward high
motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements with single-joint work kept to a small share
of volume (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13`, `week1-lecture.md p.31`). **Inference:** this
framework gives the underlying biomechanical reasoning for that weighting: whole-system,
chain-level exercises train the sequencing and joint-angle coordination that a sport skill
actually needs, while isolated single-joint work only trains the narrower kinematic-pair
level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive analysis taxonomy, not a
prescription that single-joint (kinematic-pair) work has no value; the book's own material
elsewhere treats isolated joint-angle training as informative for identifying weak links
(see [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). Do
not use "kinematic system" language as a stand-in for real coaching observation: the text
itself notes the mechanisms at the chain and system levels are "the same," differing only in
the number of interacting muscle groups, so system-level claims should be checked against
the same chain-level evidence rather than treated as a separate, more rigorously established
category.

**Example** — A leg-extension machine trains at the kinematic-pair level (single knee
joint, fixed angle range); a back squat trains at the kinematic-chain level (hip, knee, and
ankle sequenced together); a football offensive lineman's drive block trains at the
kinematic-system level (legs, torso, and arms coordinated as one unit against an external
opponent), and no amount of leg-extension or even squat work alone can be assumed to fully
transfer to that system-level skill.

**Related** — [[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]].

**What it is** — The authors organize movement analysis into three nested levels of
increasing complexity (PDF pp. 112-116, printed pp. 101-105): the **kinematic pair** (a
single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the

force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base); at the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms
extend across a larger number of interacting muscle groups, chiefly the legs and torso
followed by the shoulder girdle.

**Why it works** — The author gives a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, he attributes the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level; Semyenov and Tatyanov (1976, printed 104) found a smaller

clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even

# Three Levels for Analyzing a Movement: Kinematic Pair, Kinematic Chain, Kinematic System

**What it is** — The authors organize movement analysis into three nested levels of
increasing complexity (PDF pp. 112-116, printed pp. 101-105): the **kinematic pair** (a
single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the
**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base). Two resulting-force-less-than-sum examples the text flags
as not yet adequately analysed in the sporting literature (printed 103-104): (a) in
isolated elbow flexion, strength peaks isometrically near 90 degrees, but with simultaneous
shoulder extension and elbow flexion (stretching work), maximum isometric force shifts to
about 160 degrees at the elbow, and with propulsive work through the whole upper extremity,
maximal force develops with the elbow near full flexion, near the beginning of the push-off
(Campney & Wehr 1965); (b) with isolated knee extension, maximal force occurs in the
80-130 degree range, but with propulsive work through hip and knee together, maximal force
occurs near full hip extension and a knee angle close to 160 degrees (Dorofeyev 1965;
Yegorov 1966). At the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms extend across a larger
number of interacting muscle groups; "the only difference is in the number of functionally
interacting muscle groups," involving chiefly the strongest muscle groups of the legs and
torso, followed by the shoulder girdle. The process of perfecting movement from the
kinematic-pair level to the system level "is closely associated with the efficient
organisation and control of the motor action" (printed 105).

**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, they attribute the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to decide what level of analysis (and therefore what
level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level; Semyenov and Tatyanov (1976, printed 104) found a smaller
correlation between running and jumping performance and individual joint torques of the
lower extremity than between that performance and the force produced by the whole limb, a
correlation that strengthens further with proficiency. A compound lift like a
clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even
single-chain exercise. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection is already organized on a
general-to-specific spectrum (general preparation, specific preparation, specific
development, competitive exercises, per Bondarchuk) and weighted toward high
motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements with single-joint work kept to a small share
of volume (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13`, `week1-lecture.md p.31`). **Inference:** this
framework gives the underlying biomechanical reasoning for that weighting: whole-system,
chain-level exercises train the sequencing and joint-angle coordination that a sport skill
actually needs, while isolated single-joint work only trains the narrower kinematic-pair
level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive analysis taxonomy, not a
prescription that single-joint (kinematic-pair) work has no value; the book's own material
elsewhere treats isolated joint-angle training as informative for identifying weak links
(see [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). Do
not use "kinematic system" language as a stand-in for real coaching observation: the text
itself says the only difference between the chain and system levels "is in the number of
functionally interacting muscle groups" (printed 105), so system-level claims should be
checked against the same chain-level evidence rather than treated as a separate, more
rigorously established category.

**Example** — **Inference:** a leg-extension machine trains at the kinematic-pair level
(single knee joint, fixed angle range); a back squat trains at the kinematic-chain level
(hip, knee, and ankle sequenced together); a football offensive lineman's drive block
trains at the kinematic-system level (legs, torso, and arms coordinated as one unit against
an external opponent), and no amount of leg-extension or even squat work alone can be
assumed to fully transfer to that system-level skill. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]].

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; Verkhoshansky reports that Siff's own research at the University of the
Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under non-isokinetic dynamic
conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the resulting dynamic force-angle
curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves obtained statically. The curve
profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and joint orientation: for example,
maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance) elbow flexion does not occur near
90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full flexion, and evoking the myotatic
stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension produces yet another profile. The
same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves versus curves measured under
unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in the chapter, Verkhoshansky
states directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are unable to measure functional
maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive strength," so it is "futile" to use
them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on sporting preparedness or progress. (PDF
pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15.)

**Why it works** — Isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular
velocity, removing the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage/release, and
multi-joint coordination that dynamic sporting movements actually use; a device that
constrains those variables necessarily measures a different quality than the unconstrained,
explosive, multi-joint action it is often used to represent.

# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; Verkhoshansky reports that Siff's own research at the University of the
Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under non-isokinetic dynamic
conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the resulting dynamic force-angle
curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves obtained statically. The curve
profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and joint orientation: for example,
maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance) elbow flexion does not occur near
90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full flexion, and evoking the myotatic
stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension produces yet another profile. The
same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves versus curves measured under
unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in the chapter, Verkhoshansky
states directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are unable to measure functional
maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive strength," so it is "futile" to use
them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on sporting preparedness or progress. (PDF
pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15.)

**Why it works** — Isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular
velocity, removing the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage/release, and
multi-joint coordination that dynamic sporting movements actually use; a device that
constrains those variables necessarily measures a different quality than the unconstrained,
explosive, multi-joint action it is often used to represent.

**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the department runs the isometric seated calf raise and
other isometric tests on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed
90-degree ankle/knee position (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has
no value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
establish real, useful findings (e.g.
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance." The
caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests to infer dynamic,
functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all.

**Example** — An athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak with a slow rate of force development, or measured
at the wrong joint angle for the sport skill, can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive
performance.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1).

# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; the authors report that Siff and mechanical-engineering students at the
University of the Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under
non-isokinetic dynamic conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the
resulting dynamic force-angle curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves
obtained statically. The curve profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and
joint orientation: for example, maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance)
elbow flexion does not occur near 90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full
flexion, and evoking the myotatic stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension
produces yet another profile. The same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves
versus curves measured under unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in
the chapter, the authors state directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are
unable to measure functional maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive
strength," so it is "futile" to use them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on
sporting preparedness or progress (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed
p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15). This "futile" statement sits against the book's own
practice elsewhere: it computes explosive strength (Se) from isometric tension, "0.5 Fmax
over its time" (printed 102, 108); calls starting strength "always produced under
conditions of isometric muscle action" and says that fact "dispels the opinion that ...
isometric training should be completely abandoned" (printed 109); and builds the
functional/polyfunctional profile in part from "explosive-isometric muscular tension"
(printed 111-112, see
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). The text
does not reconcile the "futile" statement with these uses; this entry does not resolve it
either.

**Why it works** — The authors' own stated reason, given for the force-angle curve
specifically, is that curves are "determined by the type of muscle contraction, the
velocity of movement, the starting conditions, the load and the orientation of the joint"
(printed 103). **Inference:** a broader mechanism (not stated in the text) is that
isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular velocity, removing
the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage and release, and multi-joint coordination
that dynamic sporting movements actually use.

**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the isometric seated calf raise is run on the
ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed 90-degree ankle/knee position
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has
no value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
establish real, useful findings (e.g.
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance." The
caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests to infer dynamic,
functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all.

**Example** — An athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak with a slow rate of force development, or measured
at the wrong joint angle for the sport skill, can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive
performance.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1).

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky defines the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
training means (see later chapters) should target which component: e.g. a movement that
depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) calls for plyometric or reactive
methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force (component 1) calls for
more conventional strength methods. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
lever.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — The authors define the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of

force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning

linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
