# Whether a Sport Rewards Fast Force (RFD) or Total Force/Momentum Should Decide Whether You Train Max Strength or Explosive Strength

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky illustrates with a thought experiment (Fig 2.14-2.15): two
athletes perform a maximal single repetition of the same exercise as fast as possible, then
hold the load until fatigue. Athlete B produces a greater maximum force and sustains force
longer overall (greater area under the curve, i.e. greater momentum and muscle endurance).
Athlete A, however, produces *more* force than B at any early instant before a crossover time
T2 (i.e. a faster Rate of Force Development). If the sport requires rapid RFD (jumping,
striking, throwing sports such as basketball, martial arts, track and field), athlete A has
the advantage, and training aimed at increasing athlete B's maximal strength or muscle bulk
would be "misdirected" for that goal; that athlete instead needs explosive-strength (RFD)
training. If the sport instead requires high maximal force or momentum regardless of timing
(wrestling, powerlifting, rugby scrumming, judo), athlete B has the advantage, and athlete A
will not improve without training to increase maximal strength. (PDF pp. 120-121, printed pp.
109-110.)

**Why it works** — Maximal force and Rate of Force Development are separable qualities
because most sporting actions occur inside a limited time window; an athlete can be strong
in the sense of high peak force yet slow to reach it, or fast to reach a moderate force level
without a high ceiling. Matching training to which of these two qualities the sport actually
uses avoids spending training time raising a quality (say, 1RM strength) that the sport's time
constraints never let the athlete express (see
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]], Chapter 1, for the
underlying, broadly-replicated basis of this distinction).

**When to apply** — Use this as a first screening question when assigning a training
emphasis: does this athlete's sport-critical action reward reaching a given force level fast
(most acyclic, ballistic, and reactive football actions: block shed, first-step acceleration,
change of direction) or reward sustained/maximal force output regardless of speed
(sustained drive-block engagement, some wrestling-style contact)? **Eric's baseline:** force
plate reporting already separates driver metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force) from
strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations) under the ODSF framework rather than reporting a
single peak-force number (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"
citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this principle supports reading those driver and
strategy metrics specifically for RFD-type signal (how fast, not just how much) when deciding
whether an athlete's programming should lean toward explosive-strength or maximal-strength
work.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a two-athlete illustration, not a controlled
study, and most football positions and actions are not purely RFD-limited or purely
force/momentum-limited; a single football play often requires both (e.g. an offensive lineman
needs fast initial force application off the snap AND sustained drive force through the
block). Do not use this principle to justify training only one quality at the expense of the
other for a position that plainly needs both; use it to set relative emphasis, not to
eliminate either quality from a program.

**Example** — A cornerback whose sport-critical actions (backpedal-to-break, closing speed)
are almost entirely time-limited would, per this principle, get more value from
explosive-strength/RFD-focused training than from chasing a higher back squat 1RM once a
baseline strength level is established; a nose tackle whose job includes anchoring against
sustained double-team drive would get more value from continuing to raise maximal strength.

**Related** — [[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]] (Chapter 1).

running 12.1s versus 12.4s), the authors extend this to a **functional profile**
(sometimes called a "polyfunctional profile"), which adds the sport-relevant *speed*
qualities of each muscle group on top of the raw strength topography: specifically, the

groups are underdeveloped relative to a sport's typical topography, which a single
whole-body strength number cannot show; adding the speed-of-development dimension captures
why two athletes with equal peak strength can still differ in performance, since the sport

# Map an Athlete's Strength "Topography" (Dynamometric/Functional Profile) to Find Underdeveloped Muscle Groups

**What it is** — Citing Uflyand (1965) and his own data, Verkhoshansky describes building a
**dynamometric profile**: a visual map of the maximal strength of a representative set of
muscle groups for a given athlete (Fig 2.16 shows this for high jump versus distance running,
across trunk extension/flexion, thigh extension, ankle plantar/dorsiflexion). A **general
dynamometric profile**, built across many athletes of one specialization, characterizes the
strength topography typical of that sport and is preserved as sports mastery increases within
that group (Semyenov et al, 1971), though the exact rate of development for individual muscle
groups still varies. Because athletes with near-identical dynamometric profiles can still
produce very different competitive results (e.g. two sprinters with equal relative strength
running 12.1s versus 12.4s), Verkhoshansky extends this to a **functional profile**
(sometimes called a "polyfunctional profile"), which adds the sport-relevant *speed*
qualities of each muscle group (how fast each group develops working force, not just its
peak) on top of the raw strength topography. (PDF pp. 121-123, printed pp. 110-112, Figs
2.16-2.18.)

**Why it works** — A profile organized by muscle group and quality (strength peak, and
separately, speed of force development) exposes which specific groups are underdeveloped
relative to a sport's typical topography, which a single whole-body strength number cannot
show; adding the speed-of-development dimension captures why two athletes with equal peak
strength can still differ in performance, since the sport may reward how fast that strength
is expressed more than its ceiling (see
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]]).

**When to apply** — Use a per-muscle-group strength and RFD profile, benchmarked against
data from the athlete's own sport/position when available, to identify specific weak links
to target in programming, rather than programming purely off a general strength test.
**Eric's baseline:** the current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch,
ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis names as a real
usability problem, with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data dictionaries listed as
priority unfinished work (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2`). **Inference:** this framework is
a direct conceptual match for that stated gap: a sport-specific dynamometric/functional
profile (per position group, not just per vendor) is essentially what the Development Plan's
proposed sport-specific data dictionary would need to support if it is to identify individual
athletes' weak links rather than just report raw device output; this specific mapping is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** building a useful general profile for a sport requires
a reasonably sized sample of athletes at that sport and level to establish what topography is
typical, which most single-team programs (including a college football roster split across
many position groups) will struggle to establish rigorously; a "general profile" built from a
handful of athletes risks reflecting individual variation rather than a real sport-typical
pattern. This is also a resource-intensive, multi-muscle-group testing approach; **Eric's
baseline** elsewhere states inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data and that
data collection has to be judged on cost versus insight (`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy
and decision principles," citing `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`,
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); a full multi-joint dynamometric battery would need to
clear that same cost-versus-insight bar before being added to an already-running testing
menu.

**Example** — Two running backs with equal 1RM back squats and equal CMJ height could still
differ in acceleration if one shows a slower rate of force development specifically at hip
extension; a functional profile built from isometric or force-plate testing at each major
joint action would surface that difference, where a single squat-max or jump-height number
would not.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]] (Chapter 1).

14	# Strength Qualities and Muscle Groups Develop in a Fixed Order as Sports Mastery Grows, Not All at Once
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky terms "heterochronicity" the finding that, as sports mastery
17	grows, different strength qualities and different muscle groups develop their key role at
18	different times rather than simultaneously (his own coinage for the phenomenon, sourced to
19	his 1977 work). Two forms are described. (1) **Strength-quality order**: maximum/absolute
20	strength (So) increases from the start of training; explosive strength (Se) begins increasing
21	next, later; starting-strength (Ss) rises significantly only after that, tied to the
22	introduction of near-competition-intensity work (Fig 2.22a). (2) **Muscle-group order**:
23	which muscle group carries the "key" role for a skill shifts with mastery, e.g. in pole
24	vaulting, the abdominal muscles drive the initial pole-raising strength in novices, and the
25	shoulder flexors and elbow extensors take over that functional role as mastery grows
26	(Nikonov & Verkhoshansky, Fig 2.21); in the shot put, the correlation between athletic result
27	and arm-muscle strength drops from 0.83 (novices) to 0.73 (elite), while the correlation with
28	leg strength rises from 0.37 (novices) to 0.87 (elite) (Verkhoshansky & Purvin). A related
29	sequence is given for ankle/hip/knee starting-strength in jumpers and sprinters: ankle
30	flexors develop first (they bear the earliest, most intense load), followed by hip and knee
31	extensors, with hip flexors developing later and less intensely (they only oppose gravity and
32	one limb's inertia, a smaller demand). (PDF pp. 123-126, printed pp. 112-115, Figs 2.21-2.22.)
33	
34	**Why it works** — For the strength-quality order, the author attributes the pattern to
35	which quality receives the heaviest training emphasis at each stage: absolute strength work
36	dominates early training, speed-strength work is introduced next, and specialized, near-
37	competition-intensity work (which most directly trains starting-strength) comes latest in a
38	periodized plan. For the muscle-group order, he attributes it to which muscle groups bear the
39	largest mechanical load at each stage of skill development (e.g. ankle flexors are loaded
40	most intensely from the very start of ground-contact-based skills, hip flexors much less so,

# Strength Qualities and Muscle Groups Develop in a Fixed Order as Sports Mastery Grows, Not All at Once

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky terms "heterochronicity" the finding that, as sports mastery
grows, different strength qualities and different muscle groups develop their key role at
different times rather than simultaneously (his own coinage for the phenomenon, sourced to
his 1977 work). Two forms are described. (1) **Strength-quality order**: maximum/absolute
strength (So) increases from the start of training; explosive strength (Se) begins increasing
next, later; starting-strength (Ss) rises significantly only after that, tied to the
introduction of near-competition-intensity work (Fig 2.22a). (2) **Muscle-group order**:
which muscle group carries the "key" role for a skill shifts with mastery, e.g. in pole
vaulting, the abdominal muscles drive the initial pole-raising strength in novices, and the
shoulder flexors and elbow extensors take over that functional role as mastery grows
(Nikonov & Verkhoshansky, Fig 2.21); in the shot put, the correlation between athletic result
and arm-muscle strength drops from 0.83 (novices) to 0.73 (elite), while the correlation with
leg strength rises from 0.37 (novices) to 0.87 (elite) (Verkhoshansky & Purvin). A related
sequence is given for ankle/hip/knee starting-strength in jumpers and sprinters: ankle
flexors develop first (they bear the earliest, most intense load), followed by hip and knee
extensors, with hip flexors developing later and less intensely (they only oppose gravity and
one limb's inertia, a smaller demand). (PDF pp. 123-126, printed pp. 112-115, Figs 2.21-2.22.)

**Why it works** — For the strength-quality order, the author attributes the pattern to
which quality receives the heaviest training emphasis at each stage: absolute strength work
dominates early training, speed-strength work is introduced next, and specialized, near-
competition-intensity work (which most directly trains starting-strength) comes latest in a
periodized plan. For the muscle-group order, he attributes it to which muscle groups bear the
largest mechanical load at each stage of skill development (e.g. ankle flexors are loaded
most intensely from the very start of ground-contact-based skills, hip flexors much less so,
since they only move a single limb against gravity).

significantly, tied specifically to near-competition-intensity sport-specific work rather

may be leaving starting-strength underdeveloped without adding sport-specific,
near-competition-intensity exposure.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from a small number of Soviet single-sport case studies
(pole vault, shot put, plus unnamed jumpers/sprinters), not a broad multi-sport sample;
**Inference:** do not assume the exact muscle-group sequence (e.g. ankle before hip before
knee) generalizes unchanged to football-specific skills, which load the ankle, hip, and knee

working force ... is most important" (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114), which does not obviously

14	# A Sprinter's Absolute Leg Strength Has No Direct Correlation With Running Speed, but Connects to It Indirectly Through Jump Performance
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky states there is no significant direct connection between
17	running speed and a sprinter's absolute leg strength, and that this connection is in fact
18	negative at the partial-correlation level (i.e., once other factors are controlled for, more
19	absolute leg strength is weakly associated with less speed). However, there is a real, close
20	connection between absolute leg strength and jumping-exercise performance, and jumping
21	performance is in turn closely connected to running speed, so leg strength connects to sprint
22	speed indirectly through jump ability (Fig 2.23b). He extends the chain further with a
23	worked example: there is no direct significant connection between vertical jump height (h)
24	and absolute leg strength (So), but absolute strength determines the maximal force of the
25	take-off (Fmax), which determines the impulse of the push-off (F times t), which determines
26	jump height. (PDF p. 129, printed p. 118.)
27	
28	**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author gives the mechanical chain explicitly for the
29	jump example (absolute strength to maximal takeoff force to impulse to jump height) but does
30	not spell out why sprint speed itself fails to connect *directly* to leg strength; a plausible
31	reading, consistent with
32	[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1), is that sprinting at speed
33	uses leg strength at very different joint angles, contraction velocities, and ground-contact
34	times than a strength test measures, so raw strength predicts the shared underlying capacity
35	(impulse production) better than it predicts the sport skill (running speed) directly.
36	
37	**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against expecting a simple squat-max-to-sprint-time
38	correlation, and instead track a mediating measure (jump height, jump-derived impulse or
39	power) as the more direct bridge between weight-room strength gains and sprint performance.
40	**Eric's baseline:** the Baylor Sport Assessment Table already pairs strength and jump/sprint
41	measures within the same sport-specific battery (CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower
42	strength estimation, linear sprint), rather than testing strength or speed alone
43	(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
44	`update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md`). **Inference:** this claim supports reading
45	jump metrics specifically as the connective tissue between a strength-training block's
46	results and expected sprint carryover, and argues against treating a stalled 40-yard-dash
47	time as evidence that more strength work is needed if jump metrics (the more directly
48	connected quality) haven't moved either.
49	
50	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab, Soviet-era correlational finding
51	(Verkhoshansky, 1977), not a controlled intervention study, and does not establish that
52	increasing absolute strength has no *causal* value for sprint speed, only that the two are
53	not directly, statistically connected in the samples studied; **Inference:** modern sprint
54	literature is genuinely mixed on how much heavy strength training transfers to sprint speed
55	at different training ages, and some modern sources treat this relationship as more

58	modern consensus. Do not use it to justify dropping strength training for speed-dependent
59	athletes; the mediating chain (strength to jump to speed) still requires the strength link to
60	function.

63	in CMJ height or jump-derived impulse would not be expected, per this claim, to see much

14	# Four Ways Two Motor Abilities Can Be "Connected": General/Partial, Essential/Non-Essential, Positive/Negative, Direct/Indirect
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Verkhoshansky 1970/1972, Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974,
17	Khodykin 1976) gives a four-axis taxonomy for describing how any two motor abilities relate
18	to each other statistically and functionally: **general vs. partial** (a general connection
19	is the interaction between two abilities including the influence of all other abilities; a
20	partial connection isolates the interaction between just those two, controlling for others;
21	partial contribution is "the most typical case" lower than general, and partial connections
22	between the same two abilities tend to be more stable across different sports than general
23	ones); **essential vs. non-essential** (essential connections are those without which
24	efficient sporting action is impossible, and are more stable than non-essential/spurious
25	connections that may help or hurt efficiency incidentally); **positive vs. negative** (one
26	ability assists or hinders another; positive connections are most typical at the general
27	level, but a positive general-level connection can become negative at the partial level, e.g.
28	short- and long-distance running, or absolute strength versus speed of movement against small
29	resistance, are repeatedly found negatively connected); and **direct vs. indirect** (a direct
30	connection links two abilities themselves; an indirect connection links them only through a
31	third ability C, with no significant direct correlation between A and B themselves). (PDF pp.
32	128-131, printed pp. 117-120, Fig 2.23.)
33	
34	**Why it works** — The author does not give a unifying physiological mechanism for why
35	these four connection types exist; they are presented as an empirically-derived correlational
36	taxonomy from factor-analytic and correlational studies of athletes across sports and
37	qualification levels. **Inference:** the general/partial and direct/indirect distinctions are
38	essentially statistical control concepts (does a relationship survive when a third variable
39	is accounted for), while the essential/non-essential and positive/negative distinctions
40	describe the practical, coaching-relevant consequence of that relationship for training
41	transfer.
42	
43	**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to interpret why a strength test doesn't correlate with
44	a performance result the way expected: a lack of a *direct* correlation does not rule out a
45	meaningful *indirect* connection through a mediating quality (see the worked example in
46	[[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]).
47	**Inference:** before concluding "strength doesn't matter for this skill" from a flat direct
48	correlation, check whether an indirect path through a more proximate quality (power, RFD,
49	technical efficiency) exists.
50	
51	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this taxonomy describes correlational patterns from
52	Soviet-era multi-sport samples, not a causal model; a "positive general connection" does not
53	establish that training ability A causes improvement in ability B, only that they co-vary
54	across athletes. Do not use "indirect connection" as an excuse to justify training any
55	quality as relevant to any outcome; the text specifically ties the useful indirect
56	connections to a plausible mediating mechanism (e.g. leg strength to jump height to sprint
57	speed, all through the shared mechanism of maximal force feeding takeoff impulse), not to an
58	arbitrary chain of associations.
59	
60	**Example** — Absolute grip strength and 40-yard-dash time likely show a weak or negative
61	*direct/partial* connection (little to no useful transfer path), while absolute leg strength
62	and sprint speed show no useful *direct* connection but a real *indirect* one, mediated
63	through jumping ability (see linked claim below).
64

66	[[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]],
67	[[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]],

# Four Ways Two Motor Abilities Can Be "Connected": General/Partial, Essential/Non-Essential, Positive/Negative, Direct/Indirect

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Verkhoshansky 1970/1972, Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974,
Khodykin 1976) gives a four-axis taxonomy for describing how any two motor abilities relate
to each other statistically and functionally: **general vs. partial** (a general connection
is the interaction between two abilities including the influence of all other abilities; a
partial connection isolates the interaction between just those two, controlling for others;
partial contribution is "the most typical case" lower than general, and partial connections
between the same two abilities tend to be more stable across different sports than general
ones); **essential vs. non-essential** (essential connections are those without which
efficient sporting action is impossible, and are more stable than non-essential/spurious
connections that may help or hurt efficiency incidentally); **positive vs. negative** (one
ability assists or hinders another; positive connections are most typical at the general
level, but a positive general-level connection can become negative at the partial level, e.g.
short- and long-distance running, or absolute strength versus speed of movement against small
resistance, are repeatedly found negatively connected); and **direct vs. indirect** (a direct
connection links two abilities themselves; an indirect connection links them only through a
third ability C, with no significant direct correlation between A and B themselves). (PDF pp.
128-131, printed pp. 117-120, Fig 2.23.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a unifying physiological mechanism for why
these four connection types exist; they are presented as an empirically-derived correlational
taxonomy from factor-analytic and correlational studies of athletes across sports and
qualification levels. **Inference:** the general/partial and direct/indirect distinctions are
essentially statistical control concepts (does a relationship survive when a third variable
is accounted for), while the essential/non-essential and positive/negative distinctions
describe the practical, coaching-relevant consequence of that relationship for training
transfer.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to interpret why a strength test doesn't correlate with
a performance result the way expected: a lack of a *direct* correlation does not rule out a
meaningful *indirect* connection through a mediating quality (see the worked example in
[[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]).
**Inference:** before concluding "strength doesn't matter for this skill" from a flat direct
correlation, check whether an indirect path through a more proximate quality (power, RFD,
technical efficiency) exists.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this taxonomy describes correlational patterns from
Soviet-era multi-sport samples, not a causal model; a "positive general connection" does not
establish that training ability A causes improvement in ability B, only that they co-vary
across athletes. Do not use "indirect connection" as an excuse to justify training any
quality as relevant to any outcome; the text specifically ties the useful indirect
connections to a plausible mediating mechanism (e.g. leg strength to jump height to sprint
speed, all through the shared mechanism of maximal force feeding takeoff impulse), not to an
arbitrary chain of associations.

**Example** — Absolute grip strength and 40-yard-dash time likely show a weak or negative
*direct/partial* connection (little to no useful transfer path), while absolute leg strength
and sprint speed show no useful *direct* connection but a real *indirect* one, mediated
through jumping ability (see linked claim below).

**Related** — [[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]],
[[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]],
[[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1).

14	# The Structure of Physical Fitness: Key, Specific, Non-Specific, and Levelling Motor Abilities
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (1977) models an athlete's physical fitness as a hierarchy of
17	four kinds of motor ability (Fig 2.25): the **key motor ability (KMA)**, the integrated
18	ability that most directly determines competitive success in a given sport action, produced
19	by the combined development of a **specific ability (SA)** (which directly serves the key
20	ability's productivity) and a **non-specific ability (NSA)** (which does not itself satisfy
21	the sport's specific motor demand but assists when the specific ability alone is not enough,
22	e.g. muscular strength assisting speed of movement when external resistance is high); and
23	**levelling motor abilities (LMA)**, which smooth out negative correlations between the
24	specific and non-specific abilities, improve the connection between them, and expand the
25	functional range and adaptability of the key ability. Each of the specific and non-specific
26	abilities is itself built from a set of more basic **elementary abilities (EA)**, which stay
27	functionally independent and do not get "absorbed" into the key ability, but are integrated
28	by a **specific motor programme (SMP)** into a **specific neuromuscular structure (SNS)**
29	unique to that skill (worked example for explosive strength in Fig 2.26: the SMP integrates
30	starting-strength, absolute strength, acceleration-strength, and reactive ability into one
31	functional SNS). A non-specific ability can also actively hurt the key ability: the text gives
32	excessive absolute-strength development as an example of a non-specific ability that can
33	negatively affect speed. (PDF pp. 131-133, printed pp. 120-122, Figs 2.25-2.26.)
34	
35	**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author does not explain the neurophysiological basis
36	of the SMP/SNS integration process beyond naming it; the practical logic of the model is that
37	sporting success rarely depends on one isolated quality, and treating "the key ability" as a
38	single trainable target misses that it is actually assembled from at least two different
39	ability types (specific and non-specific) plus a smoothing/levelling function, each of which
40	may need distinct types of training exposure.
41	
42	**When to apply** — Use this model when auditing a training program's coverage: for a given
43	sport-critical key ability, identify (1) what directly-specific quality is being trained, (2)
44	what non-specific "helper" quality is also feeding it and whether it's being trained
45	appropriately (not over- or under-emphasized), and (3) whether any levelling work exists to
46	resolve conflicts between the specific and non-specific pieces (e.g. general conditioning or
47	mobility work that keeps a heavy-strength emphasis from degrading speed quality).
48	**Inference:** this maps onto Eric's baseline's stated training-compatibility constraint that
49	incompatible qualities are not trained at full intensity in the same block, and that
50	compatible qualities are trained together while the rest are trained at a retention dose
51	(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
52	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`); the levelling-ability concept here gives a
53	possible mechanism for why some quality combinations are compatible (a levelling ability
54	smooths their interaction) and others are not, though this specific mechanistic link is this
55	entry's own reading, not stated in either source.
56	
57	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual model, not a measured or directly
58	testable one; the text gives no protocol for identifying which of an athlete's abilities are
59	"key" versus "non-specific" versus "levelling" in a given sport beyond correlational and
60	factor-analytic study of large athlete samples (see
61	[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]), which most single-team programs
62	cannot replicate. Do not use this model to justify adding more distinct "levelling"
63	exercises without evidence that a specific conflict between two trained qualities actually
64	exists; the model describes an interaction that can occur, not one that always needs a
65	dedicated training solution.
66	
67	**Example** — For a defensive lineman, the key motor ability might be "get-off speed and
68	initial force at the snap." The specific ability feeding it could be starting-strength/RFD
69	work; a non-specific ability assisting it could be absolute strength (helps when facing a
70	heavier blocker); but if heavy absolute-strength training starts to slow the athlete's
71	get-off (the negative-influence case named in the text), some levelling element (e.g.
72	continued speed-strength or reactive work alongside the strength block) would be needed to
73	keep the non-specific quality from degrading the key ability.

76	[[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]],
77	[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] (Chapter 1).

# The Structure of Physical Fitness: Key, Specific, Non-Specific, and Levelling Motor Abilities

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (1977) models an athlete's physical fitness as a hierarchy of
four kinds of motor ability (Fig 2.25): the **key motor ability (KMA)**, the integrated
ability that most directly determines competitive success in a given sport action, produced
by the combined development of a **specific ability (SA)** (which directly serves the key
ability's productivity) and a **non-specific ability (NSA)** (which does not itself satisfy
the sport's specific motor demand but assists when the specific ability alone is not enough,
e.g. muscular strength assisting speed of movement when external resistance is high); and
**levelling motor abilities (LMA)**, which smooth out negative correlations between the
specific and non-specific abilities, improve the connection between them, and expand the
functional range and adaptability of the key ability. Each of the specific and non-specific
abilities is itself built from a set of more basic **elementary abilities (EA)**, which stay
functionally independent and do not get "absorbed" into the key ability, but are integrated
by a **specific motor programme (SMP)** into a **specific neuromuscular structure (SNS)**
unique to that skill (worked example for explosive strength in Fig 2.26: the SMP integrates
starting-strength, absolute strength, acceleration-strength, and reactive ability into one
functional SNS). A non-specific ability can also actively hurt the key ability: the text gives
excessive absolute-strength development as an example of a non-specific ability that can
negatively affect speed. (PDF pp. 131-133, printed pp. 120-122, Figs 2.25-2.26.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author does not explain the neurophysiological basis
of the SMP/SNS integration process beyond naming it; the practical logic of the model is that
sporting success rarely depends on one isolated quality, and treating "the key ability" as a
single trainable target misses that it is actually assembled from at least two different
ability types (specific and non-specific) plus a smoothing/levelling function, each of which
may need distinct types of training exposure.

**When to apply** — Use this model when auditing a training program's coverage: for a given
sport-critical key ability, identify (1) what directly-specific quality is being trained, (2)
what non-specific "helper" quality is also feeding it and whether it's being trained
appropriately (not over- or under-emphasized), and (3) whether any levelling work exists to
resolve conflicts between the specific and non-specific pieces (e.g. general conditioning or
mobility work that keeps a heavy-strength emphasis from degrading speed quality).
**Inference:** this maps onto Eric's baseline's stated training-compatibility constraint that
incompatible qualities are not trained at full intensity in the same block, and that
compatible qualities are trained together while the rest are trained at a retention dose
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`); the levelling-ability concept here gives a
possible mechanism for why some quality combinations are compatible (a levelling ability
smooths their interaction) and others are not, though this specific mechanistic link is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual model, not a measured or directly
testable one; the text gives no protocol for identifying which of an athlete's abilities are
"key" versus "non-specific" versus "levelling" in a given sport beyond correlational and
factor-analytic study of large athlete samples (see
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]), which most single-team programs
cannot replicate. Do not use this model to justify adding more distinct "levelling"
exercises without evidence that a specific conflict between two trained qualities actually
exists; the model describes an interaction that can occur, not one that always needs a
dedicated training solution.

**Example** — For a defensive lineman, the key motor ability might be "get-off speed and
initial force at the snap." The specific ability feeding it could be starting-strength/RFD
work; a non-specific ability assisting it could be absolute strength (helps when facing a
heavier blocker); but if heavy absolute-strength training starts to slow the athlete's
get-off (the negative-influence case named in the text), some levelling element (e.g.
continued speed-strength or reactive work alongside the strength block) would be needed to
keep the non-specific quality from degrading the key ability.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]],
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] (Chapter 1).

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky terms "heterochronicity" the finding that, as sports mastery
grows, different strength qualities and different muscle groups develop their key role at
different times rather than simultaneously (his own coinage for the phenomenon, sourced to
his 1977 work). Two forms are described. (1) **Strength-quality order**: maximum/absolute
strength (So) increases from the start of training; explosive strength (Se) begins increasing
next, later; starting-strength (Ss) rises significantly only after that, tied to the
introduction of near-competition-intensity work (Fig 2.22a). (2) **Muscle-group order**:
which muscle group carries the "key" role for a skill shifts with mastery, e.g. in pole
vaulting, the abdominal muscles drive the initial pole-raising strength in novices, and the
shoulder flexors and elbow extensors take over that functional role as mastery grows
(Nikonov & Verkhoshansky, Fig 2.21); in the shot put, the correlation between athletic result
and arm-muscle strength drops from 0.83 (novices) to 0.73 (elite), while the correlation with
leg strength rises from 0.37 (novices) to 0.87 (elite) (Verkhoshansky & Purvin). A related
sequence is given for ankle/hip/knee starting-strength in jumpers and sprinters: ankle
flexors develop first (they bear the earliest, most intense load), followed by hip and knee
extensors, with hip flexors developing later and less intensely (they only oppose gravity and
one limb's inertia, a smaller demand). (PDF pp. 123-126, printed pp. 112-115, Figs 2.21-2.22.)

**Why it works** — For the strength-quality order, the author attributes the pattern to
which quality receives the heaviest training emphasis at each stage: absolute strength work
dominates early training, speed-strength work is introduced next, and specialized, near-
competition-intensity work (which most directly trains starting-strength) comes latest in a
periodized plan. For the muscle-group order, he attributes it to which muscle groups bear the
largest mechanical load at each stage of skill development (e.g. ankle flexors are loaded
most intensely from the very start of ground-contact-based skills, hip flexors much less so,
since they only move a single limb against gravity).

# Strength Qualities and Muscle Groups Develop in a Fixed Order as Sports Mastery Grows, Not All at Once

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky terms "heterochronicity" the finding that, as sports mastery
grows, different strength qualities and different muscle groups develop their key role at
different times rather than simultaneously (his own coinage for the phenomenon, sourced to
his 1977 work). Two forms are described. (1) **Strength-quality order**: maximum/absolute
strength (So) increases from the start of training; explosive strength (Se) begins increasing
next, later; starting-strength (Ss) rises significantly only after that, tied to the
introduction of near-competition-intensity work (Fig 2.22a). (2) **Muscle-group order**:
which muscle group carries the "key" role for a skill shifts with mastery, e.g. in pole
vaulting, the abdominal muscles drive the initial pole-raising strength in novices, and the
shoulder flexors and elbow extensors take over that functional role as mastery grows
(Nikonov & Verkhoshansky, Fig 2.21); in the shot put, the correlation between athletic result
and arm-muscle strength drops from 0.83 (novices) to 0.73 (elite), while the correlation with
leg strength rises from 0.37 (novices) to 0.87 (elite) (Verkhoshansky & Purvin). A related
sequence is given for ankle/hip/knee starting-strength in jumpers and sprinters: ankle
flexors develop first (they bear the earliest, most intense load), followed by hip and knee
extensors, with hip flexors developing later and less intensely (they only oppose gravity and
one limb's inertia, a smaller demand). (PDF pp. 123-126, printed pp. 112-115, Figs 2.21-2.22.)

**Why it works** — For the strength-quality order, the author attributes the pattern to
which quality receives the heaviest training emphasis at each stage: absolute strength work
dominates early training, speed-strength work is introduced next, and specialized, near-
competition-intensity work (which most directly trains starting-strength) comes latest in a
periodized plan. For the muscle-group order, he attributes it to which muscle groups bear the
largest mechanical load at each stage of skill development (e.g. ankle flexors are loaded
most intensely from the very start of ground-contact-based skills, hip flexors much less so,
since they only move a single limb against gravity).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** use the strength-quality order (absolute, then explosive,
then starting-strength) as a rough sequencing guide within a periodized plan, consistent with
the classic strength-to-power progression already in Eric's baseline: **Eric's baseline:**
off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first, with
already-strong athletes shifting more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`). **Inference:** this claim adds a further,
specific step this baseline does not name: starting-strength (the ability to build force
fastest right at the onset of contraction) is described here as the *last* quality to develop
significantly, tied specifically to near-competition-intensity sport-specific work rather
than general strength or speed-strength training; a plan that stops at speed-strength work
may be leaving starting-strength underdeveloped without adding sport-specific,
near-competition-intensity exposure.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from a small number of Soviet single-sport case studies
(pole vault, shot put, plus unnamed jumpers/sprinters), not a broad multi-sport sample;
**Inference:** do not assume the exact muscle-group sequence (e.g. ankle before hip before
knee) generalizes unchanged to football-specific skills, which load the ankle, hip, and knee
in different relative proportions than pole vaulting or shot put. The strength-quality order
(absolute, then explosive, then starting-strength) is also stated to hold mainly for "sports
where the athlete overcomes relatively small resistance, and where the speed of producing
working force ... is most important" (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114), which does not obviously
describe heavy-resistance line-play skills.

**Example** — A freshman football player early in a strength program would be expected, per
this claim, to show his fastest early gains in general/absolute strength; explosive-strength
gains (jump, throw-type output) should follow once absolute strength is established; and
the sharpest gains in true starting-strength (getting off the ball fast at the snap) should
be expected latest, once near-game-intensity technical and speed work is added, not from
weight-room strength work alone.

**Related** — [[claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (Chapter 1, the
biochemical-level version of the same named phenomenon),
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]],
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]].

Woodworth
1958; Cratty 1964, 1968; Cumbeca et al 1957; Bachman 1961; Lawther 1968; Barrow 1971;
Korobkov 1958), Verkhoshansky reports several established findings on how general physical
qualities (strength, speed, endurance) relate to each other over an athlete's development:
transference of physical qualities decreases as specific fitness increases; the transfer
mechanism is largely specific rather than general; the relationship between physical
qualities can be positive, negative, or neutral; and positive transfer between qualities in
early training can turn into negative transfer later (Korobkov, 1958). He also notes it was
often claimed that complex training combining speed, strength, and endurance work develops
each quality better than training each individually (Ozolin, 1949, 1970), but states this
specific claim's validity is examined later in the book rather than settled here. (PDF pp.
127-128, printed pp. 116-117.)

**Why it works** — The author's own explanation is the conditioned-reflex model of learned
muscular activity: training builds an extensive background of "temporary connections" that
different combinations of motor activity can later draw on, and in early training these
qualities develop somewhat separately before becoming integrated through sport-specific
movements that are structurally similar to them. **Inference:** this is functionally the same
underlying idea as the more detailed ten-dimension specificity principle from Chapter 1 (see
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]), applied here at the coarser level of
whole physical qualities (strength/speed/endurance) rather than the ten specific training
dimensions within strength itself.

# Transfer Between Physical Qualities (Strength, Speed, Endurance) Shrinks as an Athlete's Specific Fitness Rises

**What it is** — Summarizing a body of Soviet and Western literature (Zimkin 1956/1965;
Zatsiorsky 1961/1965; Yakovlev et al 1960; Hebb 1949; Lindeburg 1949; Nelson 1957; Woodworth
1958; Cratty 1964, 1968; Cumbeca et al 1957; Bachman 1961; Lawther 1968; Barrow 1971;
Korobkov 1958), Verkhoshansky reports several established findings on how general physical
qualities (strength, speed, endurance) relate to each other over an athlete's development:
transference of physical qualities decreases as specific fitness increases; the transfer
mechanism is largely specific rather than general; the relationship between physical
qualities can be positive, negative, or neutral; and positive transfer between qualities in
early training can turn into negative transfer later (Korobkov, 1958). He also notes it was
often claimed that complex training combining speed, strength, and endurance work develops
each quality better than training each individually (Ozolin, 1949, 1970), but states this
specific claim's validity is examined later in the book rather than settled here. (PDF pp.
127-128, printed pp. 116-117.)

**Why it works** — The author's own explanation is the conditioned-reflex model of learned
muscular activity: training builds an extensive background of "temporary connections" that
different combinations of motor activity can later draw on, and in early training these
qualities develop somewhat separately before becoming integrated through sport-specific
movements that are structurally similar to them. **Inference:** this is functionally the same
underlying idea as the more detailed ten-dimension specificity principle from Chapter 1 (see
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]), applied here at the coarser level of
whole physical qualities (strength/speed/endurance) rather than the ten specific training
dimensions within strength itself.

**When to apply** — Use this as the rationale for reducing reliance on general physical
qualities (e.g. general conditioning, general strength) as an athlete advances, and shifting
training emphasis toward sport-specific expressions of those qualities as specific fitness
rises. **Eric's baseline:** the department already sequences training from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk) rather than treating "sport specific" as a single category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this claim supports that same general-to-specific sequencing logic, and adds the caution that
positive transfer seen in an athlete's early training years should not be assumed to persist
unchanged as that athlete advances; a quality that helped early on can plateau in usefulness,
or even work against continued improvement, later.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the "complex training" question (whether training
speed, strength, and endurance together beats training them separately) is explicitly left
unresolved in this passage; do not cite this section as evidence for or against combined
training methods, since the author himself defers that judgment to later chapters not yet
ingested. This claim is also a summary of an older, mixed literature base spanning several
decades and traditions (1920s-1970s), not a single controlled study; treat the general
direction (transfer shrinks with rising specificity) as the useful takeaway rather than any
precise magnitude.

**Example** — A young multi-sport high-school athlete's general strength and conditioning
work is likely to transfer broadly across several sports; the same general strength and
conditioning work in a veteran college athlete already near the ceiling of his sport-specific
qualities is expected, per this claim, to transfer far less, and may need to be replaced by
increasingly sport- and position-specific training to keep producing gains.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Chapter 1).

# Transfer Between Physical Qualities (Strength, Speed, Endurance) Shrinks as an Athlete's Specific Fitness Rises

**What it is** — Summarizing a body of Soviet and Western literature (Zimkin 1956/1965;
Zatsiorsky 1961/1965; Yakovlev et al 1960; Hebb 1949; Lindeburg 1949; Nelson 1957; Woodworth
1958; Cratty 1964, 1968; Cumbeca et al 1957; Bachman 1961; Lawther 1968; Barrow 1971;
Korobkov 1958), the authors report several established findings on how general physical
qualities (strength, speed, endurance) relate to each other over an athlete's development:
transference of physical qualities decreases as specific fitness increases; the transfer
mechanism is largely specific rather than general; the relationship between physical
qualities can be positive, negative, or neutral; and positive transfer between qualities in
early training can turn into negative transfer later (Korobkov, 1958). They also note it was
often claimed that complex training combining speed, strength, and endurance work develops
each quality better than training each individually (Ozolin, 1949, 1970), but state this
specific claim's validity is examined later in the book rather than settled here. The
following paragraph states a related but separate point, in tension with the above: "the
development of each quality positively influences the development of the others," and a lag
in developing one or more qualities "limits the development of the others" (Krestovnikov
1951; Kaledin 1961; printed 116). This is about qualities supporting each other's
development, not about transfer shrinking as specific fitness rises; the text does not
reconcile the two points, and this entry records both rather than picking one. (PDF pp.
127-128, printed pp. 116-117.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why transfer specifically *decreases*
as specific fitness increases. The conditioned-reflex model of learned muscular activity is
given for the adjacent point above (why qualities support each other's development), not
for the transfer-decrease finding: training builds an extensive background of "temporary
connections" that different combinations of motor activity can later draw on; the text
states, as a training prescription rather than an observed fact, that "the training means
should develop the motor qualities separately" before combined work (printed 116).
**Inference:** the transfer-decrease finding itself is functionally consistent with the more
detailed ten-dimension specificity principle from Chapter 1 (see
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]), applied here at the coarser level of
whole physical qualities (strength/speed/endurance) rather than the ten specific training
dimensions within strength itself; this link is not stated in the text.

**When to apply** — Use this as the rationale for reducing reliance on general physical
qualities (e.g. general conditioning, general strength) as an athlete advances, and shifting
training emphasis toward sport-specific expressions of those qualities as specific fitness
rises. **Eric's baseline:** the department already sequences training from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk) rather than treating "sport specific" as a single category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this claim supports that same general-to-specific sequencing logic, and adds the caution that
positive transfer seen in an athlete's early training years should not be assumed to persist
unchanged as that athlete advances; a quality that helped early on can plateau in usefulness,
or even work against continued improvement, later.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the "complex training" question (whether training
speed, strength, and endurance together beats training them separately) is explicitly left
unresolved in this passage; do not cite this section as evidence for or against combined
training methods, since the author himself defers that judgment to later chapters not yet
ingested. This claim is also a summary of an older, mixed literature base spanning several
decades and traditions (1920s-1970s), not a single controlled study; treat the general
direction (transfer shrinks with rising specificity) as the useful takeaway rather than any
precise magnitude.

**Example** — A young multi-sport high-school athlete's general strength and conditioning
work is likely to transfer broadly across several sports; the same general strength and
conditioning work in a veteran college athlete already near the ceiling of his sport-specific
qualities is expected, per this claim, to transfer far less, and may need to be replaced by
increasingly sport- and position-specific training to keep producing gains.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Chapter 1).

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky states there is no significant direct connection between
running speed and a sprinter's absolute leg strength, and that this connection is in fact
negative at the partial-correlation level (i.e., once other factors are controlled for, more
absolute leg strength is weakly associated with less speed). However, there is a real, close
connection between absolute leg strength and jumping-exercise performance, and jumping
performance is in turn closely connected to running speed, so leg strength connects to sprint
speed indirectly through jump ability (Fig 2.23b). He extends the chain further with a
worked example: there is no direct significant connection between vertical jump height (h)
and absolute leg strength (So), but absolute strength determines the maximal force of the
take-off (Fmax), which determines the impulse of the push-off (F times t), which determines
jump height. (PDF p. 129, printed p. 118.)

# A Sprinter's Absolute Leg Strength Has No Direct Correlation With Running Speed, but Connects to It Indirectly Through Jump Performance

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky states there is no significant direct connection between
running speed and a sprinter's absolute leg strength, and that this connection is in fact
negative at the partial-correlation level (i.e., once other factors are controlled for, more
absolute leg strength is weakly associated with less speed). However, there is a real, close
connection between absolute leg strength and jumping-exercise performance, and jumping
performance is in turn closely connected to running speed, so leg strength connects to sprint
speed indirectly through jump ability (Fig 2.23b). He extends the chain further with a
worked example: there is no direct significant connection between vertical jump height (h)
and absolute leg strength (So), but absolute strength determines the maximal force of the
take-off (Fmax), which determines the impulse of the push-off (F times t), which determines
jump height. (PDF p. 129, printed p. 118.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author gives the mechanical chain explicitly for the
jump example (absolute strength to maximal takeoff force to impulse to jump height) but does
not spell out why sprint speed itself fails to connect *directly* to leg strength; a plausible
reading, consistent with
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1), is that sprinting at speed
uses leg strength at very different joint angles, contraction velocities, and ground-contact
times than a strength test measures, so raw strength predicts the shared underlying capacity
(impulse production) better than it predicts the sport skill (running speed) directly.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against expecting a simple squat-max-to-sprint-time
correlation, and instead track a mediating measure (jump height, jump-derived impulse or
power) as the more direct bridge between weight-room strength gains and sprint performance.
**Eric's baseline:** the Baylor Sport Assessment Table already pairs strength and jump/sprint
measures within the same sport-specific battery (CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower
strength estimation, linear sprint), rather than testing strength or speed alone
(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md`). **Inference:** this claim supports reading
jump metrics specifically as the connective tissue between a strength-training block's
results and expected sprint carryover, and argues against treating a stalled 40-yard-dash
time as evidence that more strength work is needed if jump metrics (the more directly
connected quality) haven't moved either.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab, Soviet-era correlational finding
(Verkhoshansky, 1977), not a controlled intervention study, and does not establish that
increasing absolute strength has no *causal* value for sprint speed, only that the two are
not directly, statistically connected in the samples studied; **Inference:** modern sprint
literature is genuinely mixed on how much heavy strength training transfers to sprint speed
at different training ages, and some modern sources treat this relationship as more
context-dependent (training age, starting strength level) than this passage implies; treat
this claim as one data point in that broader, still-unsettled discussion, not a settled
modern consensus. Do not use it to justify dropping strength training for speed-dependent
athletes; the mediating chain (strength to jump to speed) still requires the strength link to
function.

**Example** — A defensive back who adds significant back-squat strength but shows no change
in CMJ height or jump-derived impulse would not be expected, per this claim, to see much
carryover to sprint speed either; the more useful readiness signal for expected sprint
improvement is the jump-performance metric, not the strength-test number itself.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]] (Chapter 1).

# A Sprinter's Absolute Leg Strength Has No Direct Correlation With Running Speed, but Connects to It Indirectly Through Jump Performance

**What it is** — The authors state there is no significant direct connection between
running speed and a sprinter's absolute leg strength, and that this connection is in fact
negative at the partial-correlation level (i.e., once other factors are controlled for, more
absolute leg strength is associated with less speed). However, there is a real, close
connection between absolute leg strength and jumping-exercise performance, and jumping
performance is in turn closely connected to running speed, so leg strength connects to sprint
speed indirectly through jump ability (Fig 2.23b). They extend the chain further with a
worked example: there is no direct significant connection between vertical jump height (h)
and absolute leg strength (So), but absolute strength determines the maximal force of the
take-off (Fmax), which determines the impulse of the push-off (F times t), which determines
jump height (PDF p. 129, printed p. 118). This sits against the authors' own statement two
sections later, in 3.3.3: "maximum strength is the main factor determining speed of
movement" (printed 151), where they pose this as a paradox in its own right: "why [do]
experiments show no correlation between absolute strength and speed of movement, whereas
under natural training conditions with an increase in strength, there is a corresponding
increase in speed" (printed 150-151), and say the answer is not yet settled. Both statements
are recorded here as given; the text does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author gives the mechanical chain explicitly for the
jump example (absolute strength to maximal takeoff force to impulse to jump height) but does
not spell out why sprint speed itself fails to connect *directly* to leg strength; a plausible
reading, consistent with
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1), is that sprinting at speed
uses leg strength at very different joint angles, contraction velocities, and ground-contact
times than a strength test measures, so raw strength predicts the shared underlying capacity
(impulse production) better than it predicts the sport skill (running speed) directly.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against expecting a simple squat-max-to-sprint-time
correlation, and instead track a mediating measure (jump height, jump-derived impulse or
power) as the more direct bridge between weight-room strength gains and sprint performance.
**Eric's baseline:** the Baylor Sport Assessment Table already pairs strength and jump/sprint
measures within the same sport-specific battery (CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower
strength estimation, linear sprint), rather than testing strength or speed alone
(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md`). **Inference:** this claim supports reading
jump metrics specifically as the connective tissue between a strength-training block's
results and expected sprint carryover, and argues against treating a stalled 40-yard-dash
time as evidence that more strength work is needed if jump metrics (the more directly
connected quality) haven't moved either.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested**: the authors themselves call maximum strength
"the main factor determining speed of movement" elsewhere in this same book (printed
150-151) and name the contradiction with this section's correlational finding as an
unresolved paradox. This is a single-lab, Soviet-era correlational finding (Verkhoshansky,
1977), not a controlled intervention study, and does not establish that increasing absolute
strength has no *causal* value for sprint speed, only that the two are not directly,
statistically connected in the samples studied. Do not use it to justify dropping strength
training for speed-dependent athletes; the mediating chain (strength to jump to speed) still
requires the strength link to function, and the book's own 3.3.3 material argues strength
matters for speed through other mechanisms not captured by this partial-correlation finding.

**Example** — **Inference:** a defensive back who adds significant back-squat strength but
shows no change in CMJ height or jump-derived impulse would not be expected, per this claim,
to see much carryover to sprint speed either; the more useful readiness signal for expected
sprint improvement is the jump-performance metric, not the strength-test number itself. This
example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]] (Chapter 1);
[[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]],
[[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]]
(Bondarchuk entries in agreement that jump/sprint-type exercises, not raw strength alone,
carry the transfer to sprint speed).

**What it is** — The authors (citing Verkhoshansky 1970/1972, Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974,

to each other: **general vs. partial** ("a general connection is characterised by the

general or partial level; the negative connection appears primarily at the partial-
connection level, and a positive connection at the general level can become negative at the
partial level. Separately, the text also reports that a negative connection has been
repeatedly identified between short- and long-distance running, and between absolute
strength, speed of movement, and the ability to produce explosive force against relatively
small external resistance, printed 118, without stating whether these particular examples
are general or partial); and **direct vs. indirect** (a direct connection links two
abilities themselves; an indirect connection links them only through a third ability C, with
no significant direct correlation between A and B themselves). As sports mastery grows, the
connections between abilities change: triple jumpers lose some of their standing-jump
ability while their sprint speed at 30m and 100m increases; positive connections shift
toward negative primarily at the partial-correlation level; and in decathletes, the negative
correlation between the 100m and 1500m grows more apparent with mastery, while improvement
in the 400m levels this out, decreasing the 100m-1500m connection while increasing the
100m-400m connection (printed 118-119). (PDF pp. 128-131, printed pp. 117-120, Fig 2.23.)

# Four Ways Two Motor Abilities Can Be "Connected": General/Partial, Essential/Non-Essential, Positive/Negative, Direct/Indirect

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Verkhoshansky 1970/1972, Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974,
Khodykin 1976) gives a four-axis taxonomy for describing how any two motor abilities relate
to each other statistically and functionally: **general vs. partial** (a general connection
is the interaction between two abilities including the influence of all other abilities; a
partial connection isolates the interaction between just those two, controlling for others;
partial contribution is "the most typical case" lower than general, and partial connections
between the same two abilities tend to be more stable across different sports than general
ones); **essential vs. non-essential** (essential connections are those without which
efficient sporting action is impossible, and are more stable than non-essential/spurious
connections that may help or hurt efficiency incidentally); **positive vs. negative** (one
ability assists or hinders another; positive connections are most typical at the general
level, but a positive general-level connection can become negative at the partial level, e.g.
short- and long-distance running, or absolute strength versus speed of movement against small
resistance, are repeatedly found negatively connected); and **direct vs. indirect** (a direct
connection links two abilities themselves; an indirect connection links them only through a
third ability C, with no significant direct correlation between A and B themselves). (PDF pp.
128-131, printed pp. 117-120, Fig 2.23.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a unifying physiological mechanism for why
these four connection types exist; they are presented as an empirically-derived correlational
taxonomy from factor-analytic and correlational studies of athletes across sports and
qualification levels. **Inference:** the general/partial and direct/indirect distinctions are
essentially statistical control concepts (does a relationship survive when a third variable
is accounted for), while the essential/non-essential and positive/negative distinctions
describe the practical, coaching-relevant consequence of that relationship for training
transfer.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to interpret why a strength test doesn't correlate with
a performance result the way expected: a lack of a *direct* correlation does not rule out a
meaningful *indirect* connection through a mediating quality (see the worked example in
[[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]).
**Inference:** before concluding "strength doesn't matter for this skill" from a flat direct
correlation, check whether an indirect path through a more proximate quality (power, RFD,
technical efficiency) exists.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this taxonomy describes correlational patterns from
Soviet-era multi-sport samples, not a causal model; a "positive general connection" does not
establish that training ability A causes improvement in ability B, only that they co-vary
across athletes. Do not use "indirect connection" as an excuse to justify training any
quality as relevant to any outcome; the text specifically ties the useful indirect
connections to a plausible mediating mechanism (e.g. leg strength to jump height to sprint
speed, all through the shared mechanism of maximal force feeding takeoff impulse), not to an
arbitrary chain of associations.

**Example** — Absolute grip strength and 40-yard-dash time likely show a weak or negative
*direct/partial* connection (little to no useful transfer path), while absolute leg strength
and sprint speed show no useful *direct* connection but a real *indirect* one, mediated
through jumping ability (see linked claim below).

**Related** — [[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]],
[[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]],
[[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1).

to each other: **general vs. partial** ("a general connection is characterised by the
interaction between any two motor abilities, including the influence of all other
abilities, whereas a partial connection involves only the indirect interaction between two
abilities," printed 117. **Inference:** in statistical terms, this maps onto a general
correlation versus a partial correlation that controls for other abilities. Depending on
the abilities compared, the partial connection's contribution can be lower, "the most
typical case," or higher than the general connection's, and the partial connection between
the same two abilities tends to be more stable across sports than the general one);
**essential vs. non-essential** (essential connections are those without which efficient
sporting action is impossible, and are more stable than non-essential/spurious connections
that may help or hurt efficiency incidentally); **positive vs. negative** (one ability
assists or hinders another; the positive connection "is the most characteristic of the
complex of motor abilities," printed 118, without the text attaching that to a specific
general or partial level; the negative connection appears primarily at the partial-
connection level, and a positive connection at the general level can become negative at the
partial level. Separately, the text also reports that a negative connection has been
repeatedly identified between short- and long-distance running, and between absolute
strength, speed of movement, and the ability to produce explosive force against relatively
small external resistance, printed 118, without stating whether these particular examples
are general or partial); and **direct vs. indirect** (a direct connection links two
abilities themselves; an indirect connection links them only through a third ability C, with
no significant direct correlation between A and B themselves). As sports mastery grows, the
connections between abilities change: triple jumpers lose some of their standing-jump
ability while their sprint speed at 30m and 100m increases; positive connections shift
toward negative primarily at the partial-correlation level; and in decathletes, the negative
correlation between the 100m and 1500m grows more apparent with mastery, while improvement
in the 400m levels this out, decreasing the 100m-1500m connection while increasing the
100m-400m connection (printed 118-119). (PDF pp. 128-131, printed pp. 117-120, Fig 2.23.)

these four connection types exist; they are presented as an empirically-derived correlational
taxonomy from factor-analytic and correlational studies of athletes across sports and
qualification levels. **Inference:** the general/partial and direct/indirect distinctions are
essentially statistical control concepts (does a relationship survive when a third variable
is accounted for), while the essential/non-essential and positive/negative distinctions
describe the practical, coaching-relevant consequence of that relationship for training
transfer.

a performance result the way expected: a lack of a *direct* correlation does not rule out a
meaningful *indirect* connection through a mediating quality (see the worked example in

Soviet-era multi-sport samples, not a causal model; a "positive general connection" does not
establish that training ability A causes improvement in ability B, only that they co-vary
across athletes. Do not use "indirect connection" as an excuse to justify training any
quality as relevant to any outcome; the text specifically ties the useful indirect
connections to a plausible mediating mechanism (e.g. leg strength to jump height to sprint
speed, all through the shared mechanism of maximal force feeding takeoff impulse), not to an
arbitrary chain of associations.

and sprint speed show no useful *direct* connection but a real *indirect* one, mediated

# The Structure of Physical Fitness: Key, Specific, Non-Specific, and Levelling Motor Abilities

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (1977) models an athlete's physical fitness as a hierarchy of
four kinds of motor ability (Fig 2.25): the **key motor ability (KMA)**, the integrated
ability that most directly determines competitive success in a given sport action, produced
by the combined development of a **specific ability (SA)** (which directly serves the key
ability's productivity) and a **non-specific ability (NSA)** (which does not itself satisfy
the sport's specific motor demand but assists when the specific ability alone is not enough,
e.g. muscular strength assisting speed of movement when external resistance is high); and
**levelling motor abilities (LMA)**, which smooth out negative correlations between the
specific and non-specific abilities, improve the connection between them, and expand the
functional range and adaptability of the key ability. Each of the specific and non-specific
abilities is itself built from a set of more basic **elementary abilities (EA)**, which stay
functionally independent and do not get "absorbed" into the key ability, but are integrated
by a **specific motor programme (SMP)** into a **specific neuromuscular structure (SNS)**
unique to that skill (worked example for explosive strength in Fig 2.26: the SMP integrates
starting-strength, absolute strength, acceleration-strength, and reactive ability into one
functional SNS). A non-specific ability can also actively hurt the key ability: the text gives
excessive absolute-strength development as an example of a non-specific ability that can
negatively affect speed. (PDF pp. 131-133, printed pp. 120-122, Figs 2.25-2.26.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the author does not explain the neurophysiological basis
of the SMP/SNS integration process beyond naming it; the practical logic of the model is that
sporting success rarely depends on one isolated quality, and treating "the key ability" as a
single trainable target misses that it is actually assembled from at least two different
ability types (specific and non-specific) plus a smoothing/levelling function, each of which
may need distinct types of training exposure.

**When to apply** — Use this model when auditing a training program's coverage: for a given
sport-critical key ability, identify (1) what directly-specific quality is being trained, (2)
what non-specific "helper" quality is also feeding it and whether it's being trained
appropriately (not over- or under-emphasized), and (3) whether any levelling work exists to
resolve conflicts between the specific and non-specific pieces (e.g. general conditioning or
mobility work that keeps a heavy-strength emphasis from degrading speed quality).
**Inference:** this maps onto Eric's baseline's stated training-compatibility constraint that
incompatible qualities are not trained at full intensity in the same block, and that
compatible qualities are trained together while the rest are trained at a retention dose
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`); the levelling-ability concept here gives a
possible mechanism for why some quality combinations are compatible (a levelling ability
smooths their interaction) and others are not, though this specific mechanistic link is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual model, not a measured or directly
testable one; the text gives no protocol for identifying which of an athlete's abilities are
"key" versus "non-specific" versus "levelling" in a given sport beyond correlational and
factor-analytic study of large athlete samples (see
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]), which most single-team programs
cannot replicate. Do not use this model to justify adding more distinct "levelling"
exercises without evidence that a specific conflict between two trained qualities actually
exists; the model describes an interaction that can occur, not one that always needs a
dedicated training solution.

**Example** — For a defensive lineman, the key motor ability might be "get-off speed and
initial force at the snap." The specific ability feeding it could be starting-strength/RFD
work; a non-specific ability assisting it could be absolute strength (helps when facing a
heavier blocker); but if heavy absolute-strength training starts to slow the athlete's
get-off (the negative-influence case named in the text), some levelling element (e.g.
continued speed-strength or reactive work alongside the strength block) would be needed to
keep the non-specific quality from degrading the key ability.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]],
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] (Chapter 1).

**What it is** — The authors (Verkhoshansky 1977) model an athlete's physical fitness as a hierarchy of
