# Explosive Force Decomposes into Four Largely Independent Abilities (So, SS, AS, Vo)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's factor-analysis research on the force-time F(t) curve of
explosive effort (dynamic and isometric, across a range of loads and joint tasks)
identifies four component abilities that combine to produce a movement's explosive force:
absolute strength (So) (the strength ceiling, confined in this text's own usage to maximum
involuntary strength, printed 107, which the text elsewhere says is not the same as a
measured isometric Fo, printed 147); starting-strength (SS) (the ability to develop the
greatest possible force at the very start of tension); acceleration-strength (AS) (the
ability to build force as rapidly as possible once contraction has begun); and absolute
speed (Vo) (average velocity of an unloaded movement). Correlations between the
gradient (rate) components are specific: explosive-strength/acceleration-strength gradients
correlate ~84% (16% specificity); explosive-strength/starting-strength gradients ~52% (48%
specificity); starting-strength/acceleration-strength gradients only ~27% (73% specificity).
As external resistance rises, the dominant contributor shifts along the sequence **Vo > SS
> AS > So**: with small resistance (up to ~40% of So), starting-strength and absolute speed
dominate; with large resistance (>60% of So), acceleration-strength and absolute strength
dominate, with starting-strength playing a supporting role. It is also stated that training
does not change this factor structure itself, only the relative importance and contribution
of each factor (printed 131). A discus-thrower factor-analysis example (Table 3.2, thigh
extension, PDF p. 152, printed p. 141) shows **absolute strength ranking first at every one
of the three torques tested** (24.0%, 32.1%, 34.7% as torque rises): starting strength drops
from 2nd (15.4%) to 4th (11.3%), while acceleration strength rises from 4th (12.2%) to 2nd
(16.2-17.2%) as torque rises. Absolute strength (So) is essentially uncorrelated with, or
mildly negatively related to, unloaded movement speed (Vo), but the strength-speed
correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance increases. (PDF pp. 140-144, 152,
printed pp. 129-133, 141, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Figs 3.3-3.6, Table 3.2;
Verkhoshansky 1968-1980 and Masalgin 1980 EMG corroboration.)

**Why it works** — Masalgin's (1980) electromyographic work corroborates the factor split
by showing the neuromotor patterns, motor-unit recruitment, and motoneuron firing frequency
genuinely differ between the starting-strength and acceleration-strength phases of the F(t)
curve — they are not just two arbitrary segments of one continuous process but reflect
distinct neuromuscular mechanisms, with starting-strength linked to innate fast/slow fibre
ratio, printed as "Vutasalo & Komi, 1978" (likely Viitasalo & Komi, verify).

**When to apply** — Use this to choose the training zone (load/resistance range) that
actually targets the ability a given sport action needs, rather than training "explosiveness"
generically. Training directed at one component produces "very little or no effect" on the
others per this factor structure, and low-correlation pairs (SS-AS at 27%) mean starting-strength
work will not automatically carry over to acceleration-strength. The text also notes the
practical training-difficulty ordering: **AS and So are easier to improve than Vo and SS**;
the text does not say this is because AS and So are more genetically constrained, only that
they are "easier to perfect" (printed 133). **Inference:** this Ch3 material supplies a
quantified internal structure (four abilities, not just "RFD vs max force") that could
sharpen how force-plate RFD/impulse metrics are interpreted for a given athlete's load
profile; Eric's baseline lists modified RSI (mRSI) as the department's daily-readiness
marker and RFD/power among the "fluffy" ODSF metrics needing a specific rationale
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); this framework's four-component
breakdown is a candidate rationale, not a stated baseline position.

**When NOT to apply** — This factor structure was derived from specific lab tasks (leg
press, discus thigh-extension) with instrumented dynamometry, on athletes of a given era
and training background; the text notes "the relative importance of each factor... alter[s]
depending on the character and especially the emphasis of training," so the exact
correlation percentages (84%, 52%, 27%) should not be treated as fixed constants
transferable to every athlete or exercise untested. Confidence capped at supported: this is
single-researcher factor-analysis work, not independently replicated in the modern
literature available to this ingest.

**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman's punch (high external resistance, opponent mass)
should be judged mainly on acceleration-strength and absolute strength markers; a defensive
back's first-step reaction off a stimulus (low resistance, own bodymass only) should be
judged mainly on starting-strength and absolute speed markers. The same "explosiveness"
label hides two different training targets. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Ch1, the
general RFD-as-separate-limiter claim this quantifies); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, the CFmax/TFmax/Fmm ladder — a different decomposition of "strength," not the same
as this force-time factor structure); [[claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction]]
(same Ch3.2.1 dataset, the Fmax/So deficit table).

# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**: the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two characteristics
of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the field-practical form
**RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time to reach it, m is
the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Verkhoshansky's own
"reactivity test" protocol: a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after
a depth-jump from 0.4 m, unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added; jump height
and support-period duration are recorded and plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force. **Inference:** RC's specific
formula (force over time-to-peak times system mass) is not explained sentence-by-sentence
in the text beyond this general stretch-energy mechanism; the fact that it tracks support-period
time more tightly than raw force output is reported as an empirical correlation finding,
not derived from a stated causal mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); this framework is
the direct historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g) versus modern
RSI = jump height / contact time), and the load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**, which the text defines three ways without fully reconciling
them: earlier (2.2.1, printed 108) as "the explosive strength index relative to body
weight," RC = Fmax/(tmax.W) = RFDmax/W; here, the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two
characteristics of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the
field-practical form **RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time
to reach it, m is the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Despite
that formula, the text separately states that in the reactivity test itself, "the
coefficient of reactivity was determined from the length of the support period and analysis
of the mean take-off force" (printed 137), not a literal Fmax/tmax calculation; the text
does not explain how the two are reconciled. Verkhoshansky's own "reactivity test" protocol:
a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after a depth-jump from 0.4 m,
unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added (fixed absolute loads, not expressed as a
percentage of the athlete's So); jump height and support-period duration are recorded and
plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force. **Inference:** RC's specific
formula (force over time-to-peak times system mass) is not explained sentence-by-sentence
in the text beyond this general stretch-energy mechanism; the fact that it tracks support-period
time more tightly than raw force output is reported as an empirical correlation finding,
not derived from a stated causal mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); this framework is
the direct historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g) versus modern
RSI = jump height / contact time), and the load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky) protocol using a specific
0.4 m depth-jump height and 10-40 kg external loading increments on a now-dated athlete
population; the precise correlation values (R=0.95, etc.) should not be assumed to hold for
a different depth, load range, or sport population without direct testing. It is also not a
plyometric-prescription framework by itself — it measures reactive ability, it does not
prescribe how to train it (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] for
that).

**Example** — Two athletes with identical CMJ height can have very different RC/RSI:
Verkhoshansky's data implies the athlete whose reactive ability holds up (or improves) as
external load increases from 0 to 40 kg is a different training case than one whose
reactive ability only shows up unloaded — the former likely has more absolute strength to
draw on, the latter is leaning more on relative strength/elasticity.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the plyometric
training method this test is designed to evaluate); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(Ch1, a related but distinct static-vs-countermovement jump comparison for a different
purpose, estimating strength deficit rather than reactive ability).

# Strength-Endurance Splits Two Ways (Dynamic/Static, General/Local), and "Absolute" vs "Partial" Endurance Explains Contradictory Research

**What it is** — Strength-endurance (sustained muscle tension with minimal efficiency loss,
e.g. a rower averaging 40-60 kgf per stroke over 230-250 strokes in 6-7 minutes, Samsonov
1969) is classified along two independent axes. By muscular-work character: **dynamic
strength-endurance** (repeated tension without interruption in cyclic sports like running,
swimming, rowing, or repeated short-rest acyclic work like repeated jumps/throws) versus
**static strength-endurance** (sustained isometric tension or held posture, e.g. wrestling,
sailing, shooting, skating). By muscle-group involvement: **general strength-endurance**
(many muscle groups) versus **local strength-endurance** (individual muscle groups) — a
distinction the text calls significant for exercise selection, since training should target
the specific muscle groups actually driving the sport skill (demonstrated via EMG in rowing,
Lazarov 1967, and via strength-performance correlation in swimming, Shchavelyev 1969).
Separately, Zatsiorsky et al (1965) resolve contradictory strength-endurance research
(some studies found positive correlation with strength, some none, some negative) by
splitting endurance into **absolute endurance** (the overall result, ignoring the level of
underlying motor abilities) and **partial endurance** (the level of a specific motor ability
once the influence of other abilities is excluded, e.g. holding or moving a load at a fixed
*percentage* of one's own max, which typically shows no or negative correlation with max
strength, versus absolute endurance at a fixed *absolute* load, which correlates positively
with max strength). To compare partial endurance across athletes, relative (bodymass-adjusted)
static or dynamic strength-endurance must be calculated. (PDF pp. 153-155, printed pp.
142-144, "3.2.2 Strength-Endurance," Fig 3.12-3.13.)

**Why it works** — The absolute/partial distinction resolves the contradiction
mechanistically: an absolute-load endurance test is partly re-measuring maximal strength
(a stronger athlete simply has more headroom under any fixed absolute load), while a
relative-load (percentage-of-own-max) test removes that confound and isolates the
endurance-specific quality — which is why the same construct ("strength-endurance")
produces opposite-signed correlations with strength depending on which type was actually
tested.

**When to apply** — Use the absolute/partial distinction whenever comparing
strength-endurance findings (in this book or elsewhere) that seem contradictory: check
whether the test load was a fixed absolute weight or a fixed percentage of each athlete's
own max before concluding the results actually disagree. **Eric's baseline:** the
department's own testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment") already defaults
novices and most women's-sport testing to repetition-max protocols rather than 1RM; this
framework implies that comparing rep-max results *across* athletes as a proxy for
relative strength-endurance requires normalizing to each athlete's own max (partial
endurance), not comparing raw rep counts at a shared absolute load, if the goal is to
isolate the endurance quality itself rather than re-measuring who is stronger.

**When NOT to apply** — The text is explicit that "an objective, reliable means of
evaluating strength-endurance in sporting activity has not yet been devised" and that
"specialists frequently use inadequate tests" — this is a classification scheme for
thinking about strength-endurance clearly, not a validated measurement protocol. The
archer example (Fig 3.13) shows that as athletes become more skilled, the correlation
between strength-endurance and competitive results actually *decreases* (control of
muscular contraction matters more than raw endurance), so this taxonomy should not be
read as implying strength-endurance always predicts sport performance.

**Example** — A quarter-squat-hold endurance test at a fixed 100 kg for a whole roster
measures absolute strength-endurance (confounded with who is strongest); the same test
at 60% of each athlete's own back-squat max measures partial (dynamic/static)
strength-endurance and is the more isolated endurance metric.

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]] (Ch1,
adjacent programming content for endurance-strength concurrent goals).

# Strength-Endurance Splits Two Ways (Dynamic/Static, General/Local), and "Absolute" vs "Partial" Endurance Explains Contradictory Research

**What it is** — Strength-endurance (sustained muscle tension with minimal efficiency loss,
e.g. a rower averaging 40-60 kgf per stroke over 230-250 strokes in 6-7 minutes, Samsonov
1969) is classified along two independent axes. By muscular-work character: **dynamic
strength-endurance** (repeated tension without interruption in cyclic sports like running,
swimming, rowing, or repeated short-rest acyclic work like repeated jumps/throws) versus
**static strength-endurance** (sustained isometric tension or held posture, e.g. wrestling,
sailing, shooting, skating). By muscle-group involvement: **general strength-endurance**
(many muscle groups) versus **local strength-endurance** (individual muscle groups) — a
distinction the text calls significant for exercise selection, since training should target
the specific muscle groups actually driving the sport skill (demonstrated via EMG in rowing,
Lazarov 1967, and via strength-performance correlation in swimming, Shchavelyev 1969).
Separately, Zatsiorsky et al (1965) resolve contradictory strength-endurance research
(some studies found positive correlation with strength, some none, some negative) by
splitting endurance into **absolute endurance** (the overall result, ignoring the level of
underlying motor abilities) and **partial endurance** (the level of a specific motor ability
once the influence of other abilities is excluded, e.g. holding or moving a load at a fixed
*percentage* of one's own max, which typically shows no or negative correlation with max
strength, versus absolute endurance at a fixed *absolute* load, which correlates positively
with max strength). For athletes who lift the same absolute load, distinguishing between
them requires calculating relative (bodymass-adjusted) static or dynamic strength-endurance;
this is stated for that specific comparison case, not as a general requirement for every
partial-endurance comparison. Elsewhere, in Chapter 2 (printed 108-109), the text names a
three-way classification: static, dynamic, and *explosive* strength-endurance (repetitively
executing explosive effort); this section (3.2.2) instead splits strength-endurance into
just static and dynamic, with no mention of an explosive form. The text does not reconcile
these two classifications, and this entry does not either. Strength-endurance's specificity
is stated as lower than speed's, "although its carry-over from one type of activity to
another is greater" (printed 142). (PDF pp. 153-155, printed pp. 142-144, "3.2.2
Strength-Endurance," Fig 3.12-3.13.)

**Why it works** — The authors state only that different studies measured different
endurance types (printed 143), not a mechanism for why that produces opposite-signed
correlations. **Inference:** an absolute-load endurance test is partly re-measuring maximal
strength (a stronger athlete simply has more headroom under any fixed absolute load), while
a relative-load (percentage-of-own-max) test removes that confound and isolates the
endurance-specific quality; this mechanism is not stated in the text.

**When to apply** — Use the absolute/partial distinction whenever comparing
strength-endurance findings (in this book or elsewhere) that seem contradictory: check
whether the test load was a fixed absolute weight or a fixed percentage of each athlete's
own max before concluding the results actually disagree. **Eric's baseline:** the
department's own testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment") already defaults
novices and most women's-sport testing to repetition-max protocols rather than 1RM; this
framework implies that comparing rep-max results *across* athletes as a proxy for
relative strength-endurance requires normalizing to each athlete's own max (partial
endurance), not comparing raw rep counts at a shared absolute load, if the goal is to
isolate the endurance quality itself rather than re-measuring who is stronger.

**When NOT to apply** — The text is explicit that "an objective, reliable means of
evaluating strength-endurance in sporting activity has not yet been devised" and that
"specialists frequently use inadequate tests" — this is a classification scheme for
thinking about strength-endurance clearly, not a validated measurement protocol. The
archer example (Fig 3.13) shows that as athletes become more skilled, the correlation
between strength-endurance and competitive results actually *decreases* (control of
muscular contraction matters more than raw endurance), so this taxonomy should not be
read as implying strength-endurance always predicts sport performance.

**Example** — **Inference:** a quarter-squat-hold endurance test at a fixed 100 kg for a
whole roster measures absolute strength-endurance (confounded with who is strongest); the
same test at 60% of each athlete's own back-squat max measures partial (dynamic/static)
strength-endurance and is the more isolated endurance metric. This example is not in the
source. The text's own guidance is that the best way to develop strength-endurance is to
execute the competition exercises themselves under demanding conditions or in a large
volume, without excluding special strength exercises (printed 144).

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]] (Ch1,
adjacent programming content for endurance-strength concurrent goals).

14	# Muscle State Just Before a Movement Ranks Performance: Stretched > Contracted > Relaxed
15	
16	**What it is** — The state of a muscle immediately before force production (relaxed,
17	isometrically tensioned, dynamically stretched, or "shock"-stretched by rapid braking of a
18	falling load) changes the working effect of the subsequent movement. In a vertical-jump
19	experiment (no arm swing), height attained rose across four pre-working conditions in
20	this order: static half-squat start 39.0 ± 6.0 cm; after a preliminary half-squat 44.2 ±
21	5.0 cm; after a 0.5 m depth-jump 48.6 ± 7.0 cm (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970). Separately,
22	under conditions of preliminary muscular tension, subjects executed movements 4% faster,
23	with reaction time roughly seven times faster than from a fully relaxed state; the ranked
24	order of preliminary muscle conditions for fastest reaction time and movement speed is
25	**stretched > contracted > relaxed** (Smith, 1964), and a motor reflex's latent period is
26	shorter when the muscle is lightly tensed for as little as 10 ms beforehand (Person, 1965).
27	The text explicitly qualifies the common coaching advice to "stay relaxed": preliminary
28	relaxation should be understood as relative to the specific movement — eliminating *spurious*
29	tension (muscles not contributing to the task) is valuable, but optimal preliminary tension
30	for brief, explosive movements is appropriate and necessary, provided its duration is kept
31	limited (prolonging it reduces dynamic force). (PDF pp. 155-157, printed pp. 144-146,
32	"3.3.1 The Influence of the Pre-Working State of the Muscles," Fig 3.14.)
33	
34	**Why it works** — When muscles start relaxed, they are "not optimally ready to work" and
35	produce a smaller kinetic effect than their capability; preliminary tension (the
36	"anticipation tuner" of the neuromuscular system, per Bernstein) and preliminary stretch
37	both pre-load the neuromuscular system so less time/force is spent simply activating the
38	muscle before useful work begins, and a genuine stretch additionally banks elastic energy
39	recoverable during the subsequent contraction.
40	
41	**When to apply** — Use this to justify why a small preparatory countermovement, brief
42	isometric pre-tension, or short approach/depth-jump stimulus before an explosive test or
43	lift outperforms a fully relaxed static start, and to caution against blanket "stay loose
44	and relaxed" coaching cues for brief, explosive actions specifically. **Inference:** for
45	Baylor's force-plate testing, this is consistent with running both a static-start (squat
46	jump) and a countermovement/depth-jump variant in the CMJ family (per
47	`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`), since the pre-working state itself is shown here to
48	be a first-order performance variable, not just methodological noise.
49	
50	**When NOT to apply** — The specific jump-height numbers (39.0/44.2/48.6 cm) come from one
51	Verkhoshansky dataset and should not be treated as universal benchmarks; the "stay relaxed"
52	qualification applies specifically to *spurious* tension in muscles unrelated to the task —
53	it does not license generalized excess tension, and the text separately warns that
54	prolonging preliminary tension too long reduces dynamic force output, so there is an
55	optimal (not maximal) duration and magnitude of pre-tension.
56	
57	**Example** — A vertical-jump test protocol that only records a static-squat-start jump
58	will systematically underestimate an athlete's explosive ceiling relative to a depth-jump
59	variant, per this ~25% height difference (39.0 to 48.6 cm) found here — the two are not
60	interchangeable measures of "jump ability."
61	
62	**Related** — [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (the same
63	depth-jump stimulus used as a measurement tool rather than a performance-boosting
64	pre-working state); [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Ch1, the
65	elastic-storage mechanism behind the stretched-state advantage).

14	# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)
15	
16	**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
17	roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force — i.e.
18	maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
19	maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
20	differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
21	powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
22	squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg — roughly two-thirds of their maximum**
23	— producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at true maximal
24	load, and time-to-complete-the-lift increased by 282% from the peak-power load to the
25	maximal load (Fig 3.17). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The Effect of the
26	Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)
27	
28	**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism beyond noting the mismatch between
29	idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a multi-joint,
30	whole-body competition lift. **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits many muscle
31	groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties, technique
32	constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot capture,
33	which could explain why the practical power-peak load sits well above the single-muscle
34	theoretical prediction, but the book itself does not offer this or any other explanation.
35	
36	**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
37	when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts
38	specifically (this is close to modern velocity-based-training guidance for squat-pattern
39	power work). **Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this is a useful citable historical
40	data point supporting load selection in the 60-70% 1RM range for power-focused squat work,
41	though it should be triangulated against the department's own velocity-based methods
42	(Perch) rather than applied as a fixed rule, since VBT data on the specific athlete and
43	exercise is more direct evidence than this single 1988-era powerlifting dataset.
44	
45	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset from a specific competitive population
46	(elite super-heavyweight powerlifters) and a single exercise (the competition squat); it
47	should not be generalized to other lifts (e.g. Olympic lifts, ballistic movements, upper
48	body pressing) without separate data, and it does not override or replace the classical
49	25%-of-max figure for the isolated, single-joint contractions that figure was actually
50	derived from — the two describe different kinds of movement, not contradictory answers to
51	the same question.
52	
53	**Example** — Programming a powerlifting-style back squat for peak power output at "25% of
54	1RM" (the classical isotonic-model figure) would badly undershoot the load that actually
55	produces peak power output in the real lift, per this dataset's ~65-70% figure.
56	
57	**Related** — [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] (the
58	broader caution about applying single-muscle force-velocity models to real, multi-joint
59	tasks that this finding exemplifies).
60

# In Cyclic Locomotion (Running/Walking), the Force-Velocity Curve Has Three Zones, Not One Hyperbola

**What it is** — Hill-type force-velocity work was mostly done on single-jointed exercises
or isolated muscle in vitro, excluding inertia and gravity effects on the whole limb and
body. The text notes poor transfer of speed-strength abilities from single-joint exercises
to natural multi-jointed movement under real gravity/inertia loading. Kuznetsov & Fiskalov
(1985) tested athletes running or walking on a treadmill at different speeds while pushing
against tensiometers, and found a force-velocity graph divisible into three zones (Fig
3.18), unlike Hill's single hyperbola: **Zone I**, similar to the classical inverse
hyperbolic relationship; **Zone II**, where force and velocity are approximately *directly*
proportional (force rises as velocity rises); and **Zone III**, where force and speed are
inversely related again, but not in Hill's hyperbolic form. The same study also found peak
force/torque is not necessarily produced under isometric conditions, agreeing with the
Perrine-Edgerton in vivo finding described separately. (PDF pp. 160, printed p. 149,
"Contraction Speed and Strength in Cyclic Activities," Fig 3.18.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond attributing the deviation to the influence
of gravity and inertia acting on the whole limb/body system during cyclic locomotion,
conditions absent from isolated-muscle or single-joint isotonic testing; the practical
takeaway offered is that this shape lets researchers "select speed-strength exercises more
precisely for cyclic versus acyclic activities" and design training machines and force
production more accurately for each.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against applying acyclic (single-joint,
isotonic-derived) force-velocity models to cyclic sport activities like sprinting,
swimming, or cycling; if profiling force-velocity characteristics for a cyclic-sport
athlete, expect a three-zone pattern rather than a single smooth hyperbola, particularly a
zone where force and velocity move together rather than trading off.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested** because this single 1985 study (Kuznetsov &
Fiskalov) directly conflicts with the classical Hill hyperbola that underlies
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1) and is itself a
different empirical deviation from the Perrine-Edgerton in vivo curve described in
[[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] — the book does not
reconcile all three pictures (Hill's hyperbola, Perrine-Edgerton's low-velocity peak, and
this three-zone cyclic curve) into one unified model, and none of the three should be
treated as the settled, final description of the human force-velocity relationship.

**Example** — A coach fitting a simple hyperbolic force-velocity profile to a sprinter's
treadmill-resisted-sprint data should not be surprised if the mid-velocity range shows
force and velocity rising together (Zone II) rather than trading off, per this cyclic-specific
finding.

classical model this contests); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]

14	# The Strength-Speed Continuum: Five Named Zones, and Why "Strength-Speed" ≠ "Speed-Strength"
15	
16	**What it is** — Reading the force-velocity curve as a continuum from V=0 to very high V
17	identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),
18	**quasi-isometric strength** (very low velocity), **strength-speed** (low velocity),
19	**speed-strength** (intermediate velocity), and **explosive strength** (high velocity). The
20	text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
21	which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
22	development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
23	describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
24	acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
25	(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
26	lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
27	maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
28	activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
29	(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
30	and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). The text also separately notes that
31	non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
32	to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
33	Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
34	behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
35	Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)
36	
37	**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
38	mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision — it prevents conflating two
39	training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
40	different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
41	"speed-strength."
42	
43	**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
44	communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
45	strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
46	speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
47	"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline:** this refines the department's existing
48	Vermeil-hierarchy and general-to-specific programming language (`method-baseline.md`,
49	"Strength and power") by giving the strength-power continuum a finer, two-sided middle
50	category instead of one undifferentiated "power" zone between strength and speed.
51	
52	**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
53	measurement scale — there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
54	"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
55	exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
56	explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
57	sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.
58	
59	**Example** — A heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed (strength-dominant power);
60	a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength (speed-dominant power); both are
61	"explosive" in casual language, but this framework says they train different ends of the
62	same continuum and should not be programmed as interchangeable.
63	
64	**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
65	underlying curve this continuum is read from); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
66	(Ch1, a different strength-ladder taxonomy — CFmax/TFmax/Fmm — not the same axis as this
67	velocity-based continuum); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
68	(the stretch-reflex/tendon caveat that this continuum's underlying curves do not capture).
69

identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),

text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision — it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline:** this refines the department's existing
Vermeil-hierarchy and general-to-specific programming language (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power") by giving the strength-power continuum a finer, two-sided middle
category instead of one undifferentiated "power" zone between strength and speed.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
measurement scale — there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.

**Example** — A heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed (strength-dominant power);
a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength (speed-dominant power); both are
"explosive" in casual language, but this framework says they train different ends of the
same continuum and should not be programmed as interchangeable.

**What it is** — The state of a muscle immediately before force production (relaxed,
isometrically tensioned, dynamically stretched, or "shock"-stretched by rapid braking of a
falling load) changes the working effect of the subsequent movement. In a vertical-jump
experiment (no arm swing), height attained rose across four pre-working conditions in
this order: static half-squat start 39.0 ± 6.0 cm; after a preliminary half-squat 44.2 ±
5.0 cm; after a 0.5 m depth-jump 48.6 ± 7.0 cm (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970). Separately,
under conditions of preliminary muscular tension, subjects executed movements 4% faster,
with reaction time roughly seven times faster than from a fully relaxed state; the ranked
order of preliminary muscle conditions for fastest reaction time and movement speed is
**stretched > contracted > relaxed** (Smith, 1964), and a motor reflex's latent period is
shorter when the muscle is lightly tensed for as little as 10 ms beforehand (Person, 1965).
The text explicitly qualifies the common coaching advice to "stay relaxed": preliminary
relaxation should be understood as relative to the specific movement — eliminating *spurious*
tension (muscles not contributing to the task) is valuable, but optimal preliminary tension
for brief, explosive movements is appropriate and necessary, provided its duration is kept
limited (prolonging it reduces dynamic force). (PDF pp. 155-157, printed pp. 144-146,
"3.3.1 The Influence of the Pre-Working State of the Muscles," Fig 3.14.)

**Why it works** — When muscles start relaxed, they are "not optimally ready to work" and
produce a smaller kinetic effect than their capability; preliminary tension (the
"anticipation tuner" of the neuromuscular system, per Bernstein) and preliminary stretch
both pre-load the neuromuscular system so less time/force is spent simply activating the
muscle before useful work begins, and a genuine stretch additionally banks elastic energy
recoverable during the subsequent contraction.

falling load) changes the working effect of the subsequent movement. In a vertical-jump
experiment (no arm swing), height attained rose across four pre-working conditions in
this order: static half-squat start 39.0 ± 6.0 cm; after a preliminary half-squat 44.2 ±
5.0 cm; after a 0.5 m depth-jump 48.6 ± 7.0 cm (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970). Separately,
under conditions of preliminary muscular tension, subjects executed movements 4% faster,
with reaction time roughly seven times faster than from a fully relaxed state; the ranked
order of preliminary muscle conditions for fastest reaction time and movement speed is
**stretched > contracted > relaxed** (Smith, 1964), and a motor reflex's latent period is
shorter when the muscle is lightly tensed for as little as 10 ms beforehand (Person, 1965).
The text explicitly qualifies the common coaching advice to "stay relaxed": preliminary
relaxation should be understood as relative to the specific movement — eliminating *spurious*
tension (muscles not contributing to the task) is valuable, but optimal preliminary tension
for brief, explosive movements is appropriate and necessary, provided its duration is kept
limited (prolonging it reduces dynamic force). (PDF pp. 155-157, printed pp. 144-146,
"3.3.1 The Influence of the Pre-Working State of the Muscles," Fig 3.14.)

**Why it works** — When muscles start relaxed, they are "not optimally ready to work" and
produce a smaller kinetic effect than their capability; preliminary tension (the
"anticipation tuner" of the neuromuscular system, per Bernstein) and preliminary stretch
both pre-load the neuromuscular system so less time/force is spent simply activating the
muscle before useful work begins, and a genuine stretch additionally banks elastic energy
recoverable during the subsequent contraction.

**When to apply** — Use this to justify why a small preparatory countermovement, brief
isometric pre-tension, or short approach/depth-jump stimulus before an explosive test or

and relaxed" coaching cues for brief, explosive actions specifically. **Inference:** for

jump) and a countermovement/depth-jump variant in the CMJ family (per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`), since the pre-working state itself is shown here to
be a first-order performance variable, not just methodological noise.

it does not license generalized excess tension, and the text separately warns that
prolonging preliminary tension too long reduces dynamic force output, so there is an
optimal (not maximal) duration and magnitude of pre-tension.

will systematically underestimate an athlete's explosive ceiling relative to a depth-jump
variant, per this ~25% height difference (39.0 to 48.6 cm) found here — the two are not
interchangeable measures of "jump ability."

elastic-storage mechanism behind the stretched-state advantage).

# Muscle State Just Before a Movement Ranks Performance: Stretched > Contracted > Relaxed

**What it is** — The state of a muscle immediately before force production (relaxed,
isometrically tensioned, or dynamically stretched) changes the working effect of the
subsequent movement. In a vertical-jump experiment (no arm swing), height attained rose
across three pre-working conditions, besides the relaxed state, in this order: from a
static half-squat position 39.0 ± 6.0 cm; after a preliminary half-squat 44.2 ± 5.0 cm; and
after a 0.5 m depth-jump 48.6 ± 7.0 cm (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970). Separately,
under conditions of preliminary muscular tension, subjects executed movements 4% faster,
with reaction time roughly seven times faster than from a fully relaxed state; the ranked
order of preliminary muscle conditions for fastest reaction time and movement speed is
**stretched > contracted > relaxed** (Smith, 1964), and a motor reflex's latent period is
shorter when the muscle is lightly tensed for 10 milliseconds beforehand (Person, 1965).
The text explicitly qualifies the common coaching advice to "stay relaxed": preliminary
relaxation should be understood as relative to the specific movement, eliminating
*spurious* tension (muscles not contributing to the task) is valuable, but optimal
preliminary tension for brief, explosive movements is appropriate and necessary, provided
its duration is kept limited (prolonging it reduces dynamic force). (PDF pp. 155-157,
printed pp. 144-146, "3.3.1 The Influence of the Pre-Working State of the Muscles," Fig
3.14.)

**Why it works** — The text states directly: "when a movement is begun with the muscles
relaxed, they are not optimally ready to work; consequently, they produce a smaller kinetic
effect than what they are capable of" (printed 145). **Inference:** the mechanism of "less
time/force spent simply activating the muscle" is this entry's own gloss, not the text's
wording. Preliminary tension is described (citing Bernstein) as the "anticipation tuner" of
the neuromuscular system, and a genuine stretch is stated to add banked elastic energy
recoverable during the subsequent contraction, plus reflexes that "increase the force of
muscle contractility as the afferent impulses increase in frequency and intensity" (printed
145).

**When to apply** — Use this to justify why a small preparatory countermovement, brief
isometric pre-tension, or short approach/depth-jump stimulus before an explosive test or
lift outperforms a fully relaxed static start, and to caution against blanket "stay loose
and relaxed" coaching cues for brief, explosive actions specifically. **Inference:** for
Baylor's force-plate testing, this is consistent with running both a static-start (squat
jump) and a countermovement variant in the CMJ family (per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`; that family does not include a depth-jump variant),
since the pre-working state itself is shown here to be a first-order performance variable,
not just methodological noise.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific jump-height numbers (39.0/44.2/48.6 cm) come from one
Verkhoshansky dataset and should not be treated as universal benchmarks; the "stay relaxed"
qualification applies specifically to *spurious* tension in muscles unrelated to the task —
it does not license generalized excess tension, and the text separately warns that
prolonging preliminary tension too long reduces dynamic force output, so there is an
optimal (not maximal) duration and magnitude of pre-tension.

**Example** — **Inference:** a vertical-jump test protocol that only records a
static-squat-start jump will differ systematically from a depth-jump variant; the two
groups here differed by roughly 25% (39.0 to 48.6 cm), but Kozinc et al 2022 (vault,
`research-papers/kozinc-2022-...`) found only about 48.4% of 770 people jump clearly higher
in a countermovement jump than a squat jump, so individual variation is large and this
should not be read as a universal, individually-reliable difference. This example is not in
the source.

**Related** — [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (the same
depth-jump stimulus used as a measurement tool rather than a performance-boosting
pre-working state); [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Ch1, the
elastic-storage mechanism behind the stretched-state advantage).

# The Classic Hyperbolic Force-Velocity Curve Breaks Down Near Isometric, and Has Several Modeling Limits

**What it is** — Hill's classical force-velocity equation, (F+a)(V+b) = (Fo+a)b (a
hyperbola), was derived largely from isolated (in vitro) muscle. Perrine and Edgerton
(1978), using in vivo human measurement, found the curve is **not simply hyperbolic near
zero velocity**: instead of rising smoothly to an asymptote as velocity approaches zero,
force/torque takes a more parabolic shape and actually peaks at a certain *low* (non-zero)
velocity before dropping to a lower value under true isometric conditions (V=0) — i.e.
maximum torque is not produced isometrically. Above roughly 200 degrees/second, Hill's
hyperbolic relation still holds. Separately, Herzog (1996) lists concrete limitations of
using force-length and force-velocity relationships to predict individual muscle force in
practice: the force-length relation is unknown for most human muscles, is plastic/adaptable
under elite training demands, differs between maximal and submaximal contraction, differs
with which length is held constant experimentally, and differs between electrically-stimulated
and voluntary contraction; the force-velocity relation is similarly unknown for individual
muscles, differs sharply between maximal and submaximal activation, differs between
force-controlled and velocity-controlled conditions, and inadequately accounts for
stretch-related (SSC) processes — stretch-shortening/plyometric force-velocity behavior
does not follow the standard inverse hyperbolic pattern at all (cf. Bosco 1982's finding
that plyometric training lets muscle produce more force after depth-jump training). Isometric
force itself also depends on contraction *history* (higher after a stretch than under pure
isometric hold, lower after a tension release), which is not captured in standard
force-velocity models. (PDF pp. 158-159, printed pp. 147-148, "3.3.2 The Effect of the Load
on Speed of Muscle Contraction," "Limitations of the Force-Velocity Relation," Fig 3.15.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is offered for the Perrine-Edgerton deviation; the
text simply reports it as an empirical in vivo finding that conflicts with Hill's in vitro
model. **Inference:** possible contributors include the parallel elastic and series elastic
tissue contributions present in an intact human joint but not in isolated muscle
preparations, and the difficulty (noted by Herzog) of measuring true sarcomere-level length
and force in vivo, since sarcomeres do not behave linearly relative to whole muscle-tendon
length (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against treating the textbook hyperbolic
force-velocity curve as a precise predictive model for an individual athlete's real,
in vivo force output, especially near isometric/very-low-velocity conditions or for
stretch-shortening-cycle actions. It directly qualifies [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
(Ch1): the general specificity logic of that principle still holds, but the exact shape of
the curve near V=0 and under SSC conditions is more complex than the simple hyperbola implies.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is marked **contested** deliberately: Hill's hyperbolic
model remains the standard, widely-taught simplification, and Perrine-Edgerton's in vivo
curve is one alternative dataset (1978), not a full replacement validated across muscle
groups and populations. Do not use this to discard force-velocity profiling broadly — it
is a caution about precision near the isometric end and under SSC conditions specifically,
not a rejection of the underlying force-velocity trade-off.

**Example** — A force-velocity profile built from isokinetic dynamometer data near zero
velocity should not be assumed to predict true 1RM isometric force accurately, per the
Perrine-Edgerton finding that peak torque actually occurs at a low, non-zero velocity
rather than at V=0.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
general principle this claim adds nuance and caveats to); [[claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion]]
(a further, cyclic-specific deviation from Hill's model within this same Ch3 section).

# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force — i.e.
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg — roughly two-thirds of their maximum**
— producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at true maximal
load, and time-to-complete-the-lift increased by 282% from the peak-power load to the
maximal load (Fig 3.17). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The Effect of the
Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism beyond noting the mismatch between
idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a multi-joint,
whole-body competition lift. **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits many muscle
groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties, technique
constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot capture,
which could explain why the practical power-peak load sits well above the single-muscle
theoretical prediction, but the book itself does not offer this or any other explanation.

**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts
specifically (this is close to modern velocity-based-training guidance for squat-pattern
power work). **Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this is a useful citable historical
data point supporting load selection in the 60-70% 1RM range for power-focused squat work,
though it should be triangulated against the department's own velocity-based methods
(Perch) rather than applied as a fixed rule, since VBT data on the specific athlete and
exercise is more direct evidence than this single 1988-era powerlifting dataset.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset from a specific competitive population
(elite super-heavyweight powerlifters) and a single exercise (the competition squat); it
should not be generalized to other lifts (e.g. Olympic lifts, ballistic movements, upper
body pressing) without separate data, and it does not override or replace the classical
25%-of-max figure for the isolated, single-joint contractions that figure was actually
derived from — the two describe different kinds of movement, not contradictory answers to
the same question.

**Example** — Programming a powerlifting-style back squat for peak power output at "25% of
1RM" (the classical isotonic-model figure) would badly undershoot the load that actually
produces peak power output in the real lift, per this dataset's ~65-70% figure.

**Related** — [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] (the
broader caution about applying single-muscle force-velocity models to real, multi-joint
tasks that this finding exemplifies).

# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force — i.e.
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg, roughly two-thirds of their maximum**,
producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at maximal load,
and time to execute the lift "increases by 282%" (the text does not state the reference
point this percentage is measured from). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The
Effect of the Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism beyond noting the mismatch between
idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a multi-joint,
whole-body competition lift. **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits many muscle
groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties, technique
constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot capture,
which could explain why the practical power-peak load sits well above the single-muscle
theoretical prediction, but the book itself does not offer this or any other explanation.

**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts
specifically. Jandacka and Vaverka 2008 (vault, `research-papers/jandacka-2008-...`) found
lower optimal countermovement-squat loads, about 47% ± 9% for men and 54% ± 9% for women,
and concluded no single percentage fits all lifters; **Inference:** treat this book's
65-70% figure as this specific 1970s powerlifting dataset's own finding, not a fixed
modern target. **Inference:** for Baylor's programming, both figures argue for
triangulating against the department's own velocity-based methods (Perch) rather than
applying either fixed percentage as a rule.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset from a specific competitive population
(elite super-heavyweight powerlifters) and a single exercise (the competition squat), and
the book does not date the study; it should not be generalized to other lifts (e.g. Olympic
lifts, ballistic movements, upper body pressing) without separate data, and it does not
override or replace the classical 25%-of-max figure for the isolated, single-joint
contractions that figure was actually derived from: the two describe different kinds of
movement, not contradictory answers to the same question.

**Example** — **Inference:** programming a powerlifting-style back squat for peak power
output at "25% of maximal isometric force" (the classical isotonic-model figure, not a 1RM
percentage) would badly undershoot the load that actually produces peak power output in the
real lift, per this dataset's ~65-70% figure. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] (the
broader caution about applying single-muscle force-velocity models to real, multi-joint
tasks that this finding exemplifies).

# In Cyclic Locomotion (Running/Walking), the Force-Velocity Curve Has Three Zones, Not One Hyperbola

**What it is** — Hill-type force-velocity work was mostly done on single-jointed exercises
or isolated muscle in vitro, excluding inertia and gravity effects on the whole limb and
body. The text notes poor transfer of speed-strength abilities from single-joint exercises
to natural multi-jointed movement under real gravity/inertia loading. Kuznetsov & Fiskalov
(1985) tested athletes running or walking on a treadmill at different speeds while pushing
against tensiometers, and found a force-velocity graph divisible into three zones (Fig
3.18), unlike Hill's single hyperbola: **Zone I**, similar to the classical inverse
hyperbolic relationship; **Zone II**, where force and velocity are approximately *directly*
proportional (force rises as velocity rises); and **Zone III**, where force and speed are
inversely related again, but not in Hill's hyperbolic form. The same study also found peak
force/torque is not necessarily produced under isometric conditions, agreeing with the
Perrine-Edgerton in vivo finding described separately. (PDF pp. 160, printed p. 149,
"Contraction Speed and Strength in Cyclic Activities," Fig 3.18.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond attributing the deviation to the influence
of gravity and inertia acting on the whole limb/body system during cyclic locomotion,
conditions absent from isolated-muscle or single-joint isotonic testing; the practical
takeaway offered is that this shape lets researchers "select speed-strength exercises more
precisely for cyclic versus acyclic activities" and design training machines and force
production more accurately for each.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against applying acyclic (single-joint,
isotonic-derived) force-velocity models to cyclic sport activities like sprinting,
swimming, or cycling; if profiling force-velocity characteristics for a cyclic-sport
athlete, expect a three-zone pattern rather than a single smooth hyperbola, particularly a
zone where force and velocity move together rather than trading off.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested** because this single 1985 study (Kuznetsov &
Fiskalov) directly conflicts with the classical Hill hyperbola that underlies
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1) and is itself a
different empirical deviation from the Perrine-Edgerton in vivo curve described in
[[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] — the book does not
reconcile all three pictures (Hill's hyperbola, Perrine-Edgerton's low-velocity peak, and
this three-zone cyclic curve) into one unified model, and none of the three should be
treated as the settled, final description of the human force-velocity relationship.

**Example** — A coach fitting a simple hyperbolic force-velocity profile to a sprinter's
treadmill-resisted-sprint data should not be surprised if the mid-velocity range shows
force and velocity rising together (Zone II) rather than trading off, per this cyclic-specific
finding.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
classical model this contests); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(a separate, acyclic in vivo deviation from the same classical model, within this same Ch3
section).

# The Strength-Speed Continuum: Five Named Zones, and Why "Strength-Speed" ≠ "Speed-Strength"

**What it is** — Reading the force-velocity curve as a continuum from V=0 to very high V
identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),
**quasi-isometric strength** (very low velocity), **strength-speed** (low velocity),
**speed-strength** (intermediate velocity), and **explosive strength** (high velocity). The
text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision — it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline:** this refines the department's existing
Vermeil-hierarchy and general-to-specific programming language (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power") by giving the strength-power continuum a finer, two-sided middle
category instead of one undifferentiated "power" zone between strength and speed.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
measurement scale — there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.

**Example** — A heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed (strength-dominant power);
a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength (speed-dominant power); both are
"explosive" in casual language, but this framework says they train different ends of the
same continuum and should not be programmed as interchangeable.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
underlying curve this continuum is read from); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, a different strength-ladder taxonomy — CFmax/TFmax/Fmm — not the same axis as this
velocity-based continuum); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(the stretch-reflex/tendon caveat that this continuum's underlying curves do not capture).

# The Strength-Speed Continuum: Five Named Zones, and Why "Strength-Speed" ≠ "Speed-Strength"

**What it is** — Reading the force-velocity curve as a continuum from V=0 to very high V
identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),
**quasi-isometric strength** (very low velocity), **strength-speed** (low velocity),
**speed-strength** (intermediate velocity), and **explosive strength** (high velocity). The
text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). This velocity-based framing sits
against how the same two terms were defined earlier in the book (2.2.1, printed 107-108):
there, explosive strength is "the ability to produce maximal force in a minimal time," with
no velocity band attached, and speed-strength is "the ability to quickly execute an
unloaded movement or a movement against a relatively small external resistance," which is a
load-based definition, not the "intermediate velocity" placement used here. The text does
not reconcile the two framings, and this entry does not either. The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision — it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline** already names "strength-speed/speed-strength
work" as a category athletes shift toward once already strong (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`); this
framework gives the definitions behind those two already-named terms, rather than adding a
new category the baseline lacks.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
measurement scale — there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.

**Example** — **Inference:** a heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed
(strength-dominant power); a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength
(speed-dominant power). The book gives no %1RM load bands for either category; these
percentages are this entry's own illustration, not sourced. Both are "explosive" in casual
language, but this framework says they train different ends of the same continuum and
should not be programmed as interchangeable.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
underlying curve this continuum is read from); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, a different strength-ladder taxonomy — CFmax/TFmax/Fmm — not the same axis as this
velocity-based continuum); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(the stretch-reflex/tendon caveat that this continuum's underlying curves do not capture).

14	# Small Changes in Joint Position Produce Large, Specific Changes in Force Output
15	
16	**What it is** — A set of cited findings showing that limb/joint position, not just muscle
17	size or fitness, is a first-order determinant of measured or produced force: the pectineus
18	muscle's rotational action on the hip reverses direction depending on whether the hip is
19	flexing or extending (Baeyer, 1922); the sartorius can flex or extend the hip depending on
20	thigh position, and its correlation with hip flexor/extensor strength varies sharply by
21	angle (0.92 at 210° hip flexion vs. 0.41 at 90°; reverse pattern for extension, 0.86 at 90°
22	vs. 0.32 at 210°); forearm pronation reduces elbow-flexion strength by about one-third
23	(Rasch 1956; Wells 1960; Tricker 1967); and in the barbell clean from the ground, slight
24	elbow flexion reduces lifting force by 40%, a flexed trunk reduces it by 13.3%, and lateral
25	head tilt reduces it by an average of 9% (Sokolov, 1967). Separately, maximal knee-extension
26	force in a seated position occurs at a 160° knee angle (with force depending on hip angle),
27	but in a supine leg press, no difference in knee-extension force was found across a
28	100°-140° hip-angle range (Lindeburg, 1964); and knee-extension strength increases 10-12%
29	when the torso is inclined 20-25° backward from vertical in a seated rowing-style position
30	(Dorofeyev, 1965). (PDF pp. 163-164, printed pp. 152-153, "3.3.4 The Relationship between
31	Strength and Posture," "3.3.4.1 Strength Variation with Postural Change.")
32	
33	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is leverage: joint angle changes the muscle's
34	operating length and the moment arm/leverage of the muscular force relative to the joint,
35	which changes the mechanical conditions of work — sometimes advantageously (full force
36	potential usable) and sometimes as a hindrance (only part of maximal tension usable).
37	
38	**When to apply** — Use this as a quantified rationale for coaching cues that treat small
39	positional details (elbow lockout during the pull, trunk angle, head/neck position) as
40	directly consequential for force output and bar path in Olympic-lift-family and clean-pattern
41	movements, not merely aesthetic technique points. **Eric's baseline:** relevant to any
42	coaching of the clean/pull pattern in Baylor's strength programming and to interpreting
43	joint-angle-specific force-plate or isokinetic data (e.g. why a knee-extension test result
44	at one angle should not be assumed to predict force at another angle or in a different
45	exercise, per the Lindeburg finding above).
46	
47	**When NOT to apply** — These are old, mostly single-study citations (1922-1967) on
48	specific joints and populations; the precise percentages (40%, 13.3%, 9%, 10-12%) should
49	be treated as illustrative of the *existence and rough size* of position effects, not as
50	precise, universally-applicable corrections. Angle-strength relationships are also
51	exercise-specific (the same knee joint behaves differently in a seated versus supine task
52	per Lindeburg), so findings from one exercise should not be transferred to another without
53	verification.
54	
55	**Example** — A 9% strength reduction from lateral head tilt alone (Sokolov, 1967) is a
56	concrete, citable reason to coach a neutral head position during a maximal clean attempt,
57	beyond generic "keep your head neutral" cueing.
58

60	torque/leverage principle this claim supplies specific joint-angle examples for);
61	[[principle--pelvic-tilt-is-task-specific-not-universal]] (the pelvis-specific continuation
62	of this same posture discussion, 3.3.4.2).
